title: Dimension Free Theorems in Geometry
summary: Maurey’s empirical method gives dimension-free convex approximation. Gaussian projections preserve distances and approximate supporting half-spaces for finite point sets.
body: Mars-Dingdang · Original notes dated April 13, 2026 Many geometric bounds depend on the ambient dimension. For example, Carathéodory’s theorem guarantees that any point in the convex hull of a set in \(\mathbb R^n\) can be represented using at most \(n+1\) of its points. When the set lies in the Euclidean unit ball, allowing an error of \(\varepsilon\) reduces the required number to \(\lceil\varepsilon^{-2}\rceil\), independently of the dimension. This approximation is useful in the analysis of algorithms for high-dimensional data. In these notes we use Maurey’s empirical method to obtain that approximation, count the resulting cover of a polytope, and turn the cover into a volume bound. Then we use the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma to preserve distances and approximate supporting half-spaces under a linear map. Carathéodory’s theoremConvex combinations and convex hullsA convex combination of \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\in\mathbb R^n\) is a sum \(\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i x_i\) with \(\lambda_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\). The convex hull of \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the set of all its finite convex combinations: \[\operatorname{conv}(T)= \left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i x_i: x_i\in T,\ \lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1,\ k\ge1\right\}.\] Theorem (Carathéodory). Every \(x\in\operatorname{conv}(T)\) is a convex combination of at most \(n+1\) points from \(T\). Proof. Write \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\), dropping zero coefficients. If \(m>n+1\), the \(m-1\) vectors \(x_2-x_1,\ldots,x_m-x_1\) are linearly dependent. Choose coefficients \(c_2,\ldots,c_m\), not all zero, with \(\sum_{i=2}^m c_i(x_i-x_1)=0\). Setting \(\mu_1=-\sum_{i=2}^m c_i\) and \(\mu_i=c_i\) for \(i\ge2\) gives \[\sum_{i=1}^m\mu_i=0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\mu_i x_i=0.\] Since the \(\mu_i\) sum to zero and are not all zero, some are positive. Take \[\alpha=\min_{\mu_i>0}\frac{\lambda_i}{\mu_i}.\] The new coefficients \(\lambda_i-\alpha\mu_i\) are nonnegative and sum to one. They represent the same \(x\), and at least one is zero. Repeat until at most \(n+1\) coefficients remain. \(\square\) The bound is tight. The origin and the \(n\) standard basis vectors form an \(n\)-simplex. Each point in its interior has all \(n+1\) barycentric coordinates positive. Approximate Carathéodory by independent samplingTheorem. Suppose \(T\subseteq B_2^n\), the unit Euclidean ball. For every \(x\in\operatorname{conv}(T)\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), there are \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\in T\), with repetition allowed, such that \[\left\|x-\frac1k\sum_{j=1}^k x_j\right\|_2\le \frac1{\sqrt{k}}.\] Proof. Write \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i z_i\) and define a random vector \(Z\) by sampling \(z_i\) with probability \(\lambda_i\). Then \(\mathbb E Z=x\). Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_k\) be independent copies of \(Z\). Cross terms have expectation zero, so \[\begin{aligned} \mathbb E\left\|\frac1k\sum_{j=1}^k Z_j-x\right\|_2^2 &=\frac1{k^2}\sum_{j=1}^k\mathbb E\|Z_j-x\|_2^2\\ &=\frac{\mathbb E\|Z\|_2^2-\|x\|_2^2}{k} \le \frac1k. \end{aligned}\] At least one sample attains squared error at most \(1/k\). This is Maurey’s empirical method. \(\square\) Figure 1. The empirical mean approximates a point in a three-dimensional convex hull. Tightness. For \(1\le k\le n\), take \(T=\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}\) and \(x=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n e_i\). If \(u=\sum_{j=1}^k\lambda_j x_j\) is a convex combination from \(T\), merge coefficients on repeated points. Write \(u=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i e_i\), with \(\sum_i a_i=1\) and at most \(k\) nonzero entries. Then \[\|x-u\|_2^2 =\sum_{i=1}^n\left(a_i-\frac1n\right)^2 =\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2-\frac1n \ge \frac1k-\frac1n.\] The last step is Cauchy–Schwarz. Equality is attained by placing mass \(1/k\) on \(k\) distinct basis vectors. Thus even arbitrary convex weights cannot improve the \(k^{-1/2}\) order when \(n\) is large compared with \(k\). Covering a polytope and bounding its volumeLet \(P\subseteq B_2^n\) be a polytope with \(N\) vertices, and let \(k\ge1\) be an integer. Every point in \(P\) is within \(1/\sqrt{k}\) of the average of \(k\) vertices. Taking all ordered choices gives at most \(N^k\) centers. The order of the vertices has no effect on the average. Counting the possible multiplicities \(c_1,\ldots,c_N\ge0\) with \(\sum_i c_i=k\) gives a smaller upper bound by stars and bars: \[M\le \binom{N+k-1}{k}.\] Several multiplicity vectors can give the same center, which only reduces the cover size. Figure 2. A cover of a three-dimensional polytope by balls centered on averages of vertices. For a cover by \(M\) balls of radius \(1/\sqrt{k}\), volume subadditivity gives \[\left(\frac{\operatorname{Vol}(P)}{\operatorname{Vol}(B_2^n)}\right)^{1/n} \le \frac{M^{1/n}}{\sqrt{k}}.\] A first volume bound. With \(M=N^k\), \[\frac{\operatorname{Vol}(P)}{\operatorname{Vol}(B_2^n)} \le \left(3\sqrt{\frac{\log N}{n}}\right)^n.\] For \(N=1\) the volume is zero. When \(n<9\log N\), the right side exceeds one, which suffices since \(P\subseteq B_2^n\). Otherwise take \(k=\lceil n/(2\log N)\rceil\). Then \[k^{-1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{2\log N}{n}},\qquad N^{k/n}\le e^{1/2}N^{1/n}\le e^{11/18}.\] Now \(\sqrt2\,e^{11/18}<3\). \(\square\) A combinatorial estimate. For integers \(1\le k\le m\), \[\left(\frac{m}{k}\right)^k \le\binom{m}{k} \le\sum_{j=0}^k\binom{m}{j} \le\left(\frac{em}{k}\right)^k.\] For the first inequality, each factor \((m-i)/(k-i)\) in the product for \(\binom{m}{k}\) is at least \(m/k\). For the last, take \(t=k/m\in(0,1]\). Since \(t^j\ge t^k\) for \(j\le k\), \[\sum_{j=0}^k\binom{m}{j} \le t^{-k}(1+t)^m \le t^{-k}e^{mt}=\left(\frac{em}{k}\right)^k.\] Theorem (Carl–Pajor volume bound). If \(P\) is full-dimensional and has \(N\) vertices, then \[\frac{\operatorname{Vol}(P)}{\operatorname{Vol}(B_2^n)} \le \left(23\sqrt{\frac{\log(eN/n)}{n}}\right)^n.\] If \(P\) is lower-dimensional, its \(n\)-dimensional volume is zero. Proof. Full dimension implies \(N\ge n+1\). Write \(L=\log(eN/n)>1\). If \(n<2L\), the bound follows from \(P\subseteq B_2^n\). Otherwise take \(k=\lceil n/(2L)\rceil\). Then \(n/(2L)\le k\le n/L\le n\), so \[M\le\binom{N+k-1}{k}\le\left(\frac{2eN}{k}\right)^k.\] Using \(2eN/k\le 4eNL/n\) and \(k/n\le1/L\), we obtain \[\log(M^{1/n}) \le \frac{\log 4+L+\log L}{L} \le \log 4+1+1/e<2.76.\] Here \(\log L/L\le1/e\) for \(L\ge1\). Thus \(M^{1/n}<16\), while \(1/\sqrt{k}\le\sqrt{2L/n}\). Their product is bounded by \(23\sqrt{L/n}\). \(\square\) The Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemmaTheorem. For \(0<\varepsilon<1\) and \(n\ge2\), any set of \(n\) points in \(\mathbb R^d\) admits a linear map \(f\colon\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k\) such that \[(1-\varepsilon)\|x-y\|_2^2 \le\|f(x)-f(y)\|_2^2 \le(1+\varepsilon)\|x-y\|_2^2\] for every pair of points, provided \(k\ge8\log n/\varepsilon^2\). Proof. Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{k\times d}\) have independent \(\mathcal N(0,1/k)\) entries. For any fixed nonzero \(v\), \[X=\frac{k\|Av\|_2^2}{\|v\|_2^2}\sim\chi_k^2.\] Its moment generating function is \((1-2t)^{-k/2}\) for \(t<1/2\). Applying Markov’s inequality to \(e^{tX}\) with \(t=(r-1)/(2r)\) gives the upper tail when \(r>1\) and the lower tail when \(0<r<1\): \[\begin{aligned} \Pr(X\ge kr)&\le e^{-\frac k2(r-1-\log r)} &&(r>1),\\ \Pr(X\le kr)&\le e^{-\frac k2(r-1-\log r)} &&(0<r<1). \end{aligned}\] To obtain the stated constant, set \(s=\operatorname{arctanh}(\varepsilon)/\varepsilon\) and choose \(f(x)=Ax/\sqrt{s}\). The two thresholds for \(X/k\) are \(r_\pm=s(1\pm\varepsilon)\). We have \(r_+>1\) and \(0<r_-<1\) by bounding the integrand in \(\operatorname{arctanh}\varepsilon=\int_0^\varepsilon(1-t^2)^{-1}\,dt\). Since \(r_+-r_-=2s\varepsilon=\log(r_+/r_-)\), the two rate terms \(r_\pm-1-\log r_\pm\) are equal. Each is their average: \[s-1-\log s-\tfrac12\log(1-\varepsilon^2)\ge\tfrac12\varepsilon^2.\] Thus each fixed pair fails with probability at most \(2e^{-k\varepsilon^2/4}\). A union bound over the \(\binom n2\) pairs gives a failure probability at most \((n-1)/n<1\) when \(k\ge8\log n/\varepsilon^2\). \(\square\) Figure 3. The two Gaussian projections shown here go from 3D through 283D to 2D. The final panel illustrates the geometry. The theorem’s dimension bound determines when a uniform distortion guarantee applies. For fixed distortion, the order \(\log n\) is necessary for some sets of \(n\) points, even if the embedding may be nonlinear. Exercise 4 gives a packing argument. Approximate supporting half-spaces after projectionSuppose \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is a convex body containing the unit ball, and \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\partial K\). The points lie on supporting hyperplanes in the original space. Under a suitable linear map to dimension \(O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2m))\), we can place the images inside a convex body whose boundary stays within \(O((1+D^2)\varepsilon)\) of each image, where \(D=\operatorname{diam}K\). We can also keep the projected supporting directions with a comparable one-sided error. Projection onto a closed convex set. If \(C\) is nonempty, closed and convex, every \(y\) has a unique closest point \(x\in C\). A minimizing sequence for \(\|y-z\|_2\) is bounded and has a subsequence converging in \(C\). Uniqueness follows because for two different minimizers, the squared distance to their midpoint is strictly less than the common minimum. The closest point is characterized by \[\langle y-x,z-x\rangle\le0\qquad(z\in C).\] Indeed, for \(0\le t\le1\), the segment \(x+t(z-x)\) belongs to \(C\). The right derivative of \(\|y-x-t(z-x)\|_2^2\) at \(t=0\) must be nonnegative, which gives the inequality. Conversely, expanding \(\|y-z\|_2^2\) shows it is at least \(\|y-x\|_2^2\). Supporting hyperplane at a boundary point. Given \(x\in\partial K\), take \(y_\ell\notin K\) with \(y_\ell\to x\). If \(z_\ell\) is the closest point in \(K\) to \(y_\ell\), then \(\|y_\ell-z_\ell\|_2\le\|y_\ell-x\|_2\), so \(z_\ell\to x\). A subsequence of the unit vectors \((z_\ell-y_\ell)/\|z_\ell-y_\ell\|_2\) converges to a unit vector \(n\). The projection inequality then gives \(\langle z-x,n\rangle\ge0\) for every \(z\in K\). Thus \(n\) is an inward normal of a supporting hyperplane through \(x\). Preservation argument. Let \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\). Choose a unit inward normal \(n_i\) at each \(x_i\) and put \(y_i=x_i+n_i\). Apply Johnson–Lindenstrauss to the set \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_m\}\). Write \(x'_i=f(x_i)\) and \(n'_i=f(n_i)\). For each \(i,j\) the three squared distances of the triangle \(x_i,y_i,x_j\) are preserved within factors \(1\pm\varepsilon\). Polarization gives \[\begin{aligned} \langle n'_i,x'_j-x'_i\rangle &=\tfrac12\bigl(\|f(y_i-x_i)\|_2^2+\|f(x_j-x_i)\|_2^2-\|f(y_i-x_j)\|_2^2\bigr)\\ &\ge (1+\varepsilon)\langle n_i,x_j-x_i\rangle -\varepsilon\bigl(1+\|x_j-x_i\|_2^2\bigr)\\ &\ge -(1+D^2)\varepsilon. \end{aligned}\] Set \(C_D=1+D^2\). Each \(x'_j\) is strictly inside every half-space \[H_i=\{z:\langle z-x'_i,n'_i\rangle\ge -(C_D+1)\varepsilon\}.\] Intersect the \(H_i\) with a closed ball large enough to contain all \(x'_j\) in its interior. This gives a compact convex body \(K'\) with nonempty interior. In direction \(n'_i\), its actual supporting plane is attained at the minimum of \(z\mapsto\langle z-x'_i,n'_i\rangle\) on \(K'\). That minimum lies between \(-(C_D+1)\varepsilon\) and \(0\) because \(K'\subseteq H_i\) and \(x'_i\in K'\). Since \(\|n'_i\|_2\ge\sqrt{1-\varepsilon}>1/2\), the plane is within \(2(C_D+1)\varepsilon\) of \(x'_i\). The segment from \(x'_i\) to its orthogonal projection onto the plane meets \(\partial K'\) no later than it meets the plane. This yields the desired distance bound. Normalizing \(n'_i\) to unit length changes the half-space error by at most a factor of two. \(\square\) Exercises1. Independent sets by the probabilistic methodLet \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph and \(d(v)\) the degree of \(v\). Prove that \(G\) has an independent set of size at least \(\sum_{v\in V}1/(d(v)+1)\). Hint. Order the vertices uniformly at random and keep those that come before every neighbor. If \(|V|=n\) and \(|E|=m\), deduce a lower bound of \(n^2/(2m+n)\). 2. Where the mass of a Euclidean ball liesLet \(X\) be uniform in \(B_2^n\), so \(\Pr(X\in A)=\operatorname{Vol}(A)/\operatorname{Vol}(B_2^n)\) for measurable \(A\subseteq B_2^n\). Prove that the shell \(1-5/n\le\|X\|_2\le1\) contains at least \(99\%\) of the mass. Prove that \(\mathbb E\|X\|_2=n/(n+1)\). 3. The chi-square distribution and random projectionLet \(X=\sum_{i=1}^k Z_i^2\), where the \(Z_i\) are independent standard Gaussians. Compute \(\mathbb EX\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\). Derive \(\mathbb E e^{tX}=(1-2t)^{-k/2}\) for \(t<1/2\). Use the moment generating function and the logarithm’s Taylor bound to show that for \(0<\varepsilon<1\), \[\Pr\bigl(|X-\mathbb EX|>\varepsilon\mathbb EX\bigr) \le2\exp\left(-\frac{k}{4}(\varepsilon^2-\varepsilon^3)\right).\] Show also that the probability is at most \(2e^{-Ck\varepsilon^2}\) for an absolute \(C>0\) over this range. Hint. For the second bound, use \(\varepsilon-\log(1+\varepsilon)=\int_0^\varepsilon t/(1+t)\,dt\).4. Combine this estimate with a union bound to derive the Johnson–Lindenstrauss dimension order. 4. A dimension lower bound by packing If \(z_1,\ldots,z_n\in\mathbb R^k\) satisfy \(1<\|z_i-z_j\|_2\le2\) for all \(i\ne j\), show that \(n\le5^k\). Hint. Pack disjoint open balls of radius \(1/2\) around the points inside a ball of radius \(5/2\). Find \(n\) vectors in \(\mathbb R^n\) for which no map into \(\mathbb R^k\) preserves every distance to relative error \(0.01\) when \(k<\tfrac12\log n\). Hint. Try the standard basis vectors and use part 1. 5. Characterizing a closest pointGiven a nonempty closed convex set \(C\) and \(x\in C\), prove that \(x\) is the projection of \(y\) onto \(C\) if and only if \(\langle y-x,z-x\rangle\le0\) for all \(z\in C\). Try proving both directions before checking the argument above. 6. A deterministic greedy constructionLet \(T\subseteq B_2^n\) and \(x\in\operatorname{conv}(T)\). Construct a sequence \(x_1,x_2,\ldots\in T\) such that for every \(k\ge1\), its empirical mean \(p_k=k^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^k x_i\) satisfies \[\|x-p_k\|_2^2\le 4/k.\] Hint. Set \(e_k=x-p_k\). Express \(x\) as a convex combination from \(T\) and choose \(x_{k+1}\) with \(\langle e_k,x-x_{k+1}\rangle\le0\). Then bound the change in the squared norm of \(ke_k\). The choice of a point by a linear objective also appears in Frank–Wolfe optimization. In this exercise the iterates retain a sparse convex representation. 7. Sparse strategies in a large zero-sum gameLet \(A\in[-1,1]^{m\times n}\) be the payoff matrix and let \(y\in\Delta_n\) be a mixed strategy for the column player. Here \(\Delta_n=\{u\in\mathbb R^n:u_i\ge0,\ \sum_i u_i=1\}\). Given \(\varepsilon>0\), show that a strategy \(\widehat y\in\Delta_n\) supported on at most \[k=\left\lceil\frac{2\log(2m)}{\varepsilon^2}\right\rceil\] columns can satisfy \(\|A\widehat y-Ay\|_\infty\le\varepsilon\). Hint. Sample columns independently according to \(y\). Apply Hoeffding’s inequality coordinate by coordinate and count the possible payoff deviations. 8. Coresets for an SVM marginLet \(P,Q\subset B_2^n\) be two point sets whose convex hulls attain a minimum distance \(\gamma>0\). Prove that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there are subsets \(P'\subseteq P\) and \(Q'\subseteq Q\), each of size at most \(\lceil4/\varepsilon^2\rceil\), such that \[\gamma\le\min_{\substack{p\in\operatorname{conv}(P')\\q\in\operatorname{conv}(Q')}}\|p-q\|_2 \le\gamma+\varepsilon.\] Hint. Approximate one closest pair \(p_\star,q_\star\) by averages of \(k\) points from the respective sets, with \(k=\lceil4/\varepsilon^2\rceil\), and apply the triangle inequality. The result gives a dimension-independent coreset for the optimal margin value.

title: ML 14: Model Interpretability and Feature Attribution
summary: Derive the weighted fit in LIME and prove completeness for Integrated Gradients and efficiency for Shapley values.
body: Derive the weighted fit in LIME and prove completeness for Integrated Gradients and efficiency for Shapley values. The model is locally flat at the input, but the path from the baseline crosses a segment of slope one. Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic ExplanationsFor an input \(x\), sample nearby or masked inputs \(z_j\) and compute the black box’s scores \(f(z_j)\). Fit an interpretable model \(g\) on human-readable representations \(z'_j\) via \[\min_g \sum_j \pi_x(z_j)(f(z_j)-g(z'_j))^2+\Omega(g).\] The proximity weights \(\pi_x\) emphasize the neighborhood. The penalty \(\Omega\) limits complexity, for example the number of nonzero coefficients. On a fixed feature set and without the penalty, write the design as \(A\), weights as a diagonal matrix \(W\), and responses as \(f\). Differentiating \((A\beta-f)^\top W(A\beta-f)\) gives the normal equation \(A^\top WA\beta=A^\top Wf\). Kernel width and the distribution of perturbed examples determine the fitting problem. A model that is flat near \(x\) can have a near-zero local slope even when its output differs substantially from a meaningful baseline. Integrated Gradients along a baseline pathSet \(\gamma(t)=x'+t(x-x')\) for baseline \(x'\). The attribution for coordinate \(i\) is \[\operatorname{IG}_i(x;x')=(x_i-x'_i)\int_0^1\partial_iF(\gamma(t))\,dt.\] When \(F\circ\gamma\) is absolutely continuous and the chain rule holds almost everywhere along the path, summing the attributions gives \[\sum_i\operatorname{IG}_i =\int_0^1\nabla F(\gamma(t))^\top (x-x')\,dt =\int_0^1 (F\circ\gamma)'(t)\,dt=F(x)-F(x').\] This is completeness. If only coordinate \(i\) differs from the baseline, completeness means all nonzero output difference must be assigned to \(i\), giving the sensitivity property for that case. Implementation invariance follows because two identical differentiable functions have identical partial derivatives wherever they exist. For \(F(x)=\min\{\max(x,0),1\}\) from baseline 0 to input 2, the path lies in the unit-slope region for half its duration. The contribution is \(2(1/2)=1\) despite zero endpoint derivative. Numerical quadrature can be checked by the residual in completeness. Shapley values as averages over permutationsLet \(v(S)\) be the prediction-related value for a coalition of available features \(S\) from feature set \(N\). The Shapley attribution is \[\phi_i=\sum_{S\subseteq N\setminus\{i\}} \frac{|S|!(|N|-|S|-1)!}{|N|!}\,[v(S\cup\{i\})-v(S)].\] The coefficient is the probability that exactly \(S\) precedes \(i\) in a uniform random permutation: order these predecessors arbitrarily, then order all successors. For any fixed permutation, the marginal contributions telescope to \(v(N)-v(\varnothing)\). Averaging proves efficiency. Symmetric participants exchange positions through a bijection of permutations and hence receive the same average. A dummy with zero marginal contribution receives zero, and linearity follows by taking expectations. For a pure interaction \(v_T(S)=\mathbf1\{T\subseteq S\}\), an element of \(T\) receives the unit contribution exactly when it is last among \(T\). Its attribution is therefore \(1/|T|\). These pure interactions also span all games with \(v(\varnothing)=0\) by subset inclusion–exclusion, which gives uniqueness under these axioms. SHAP specifies a value function and an approximation or evaluation procedure. Examples include filling missing features with a fixed baseline, integrating over background features, or conditioning the missing features on observed ones. Correlation means these choices answer different questions. In a conditional game, a feature can get credit for information about another feature on which the model directly depends. Why Shapley weights give the unique additive attributionWrite \(v(\varnothing)=0\) after subtracting the baseline. For nonempty \(T\subseteq[d]\), let \(u_T(S)=\mathbf1\{T\subseteq S\}\). Every set function has a unique expansion \(v=\sum_{T\ne\varnothing}a_Tu_T\): recursively take \(a_T=v(T)-\sum_{U\subsetneq T}a_U\) starting with singletons. For the game \(u_T\), the null-player axiom gives zero to players outside \(T\) and symmetry forces equal shares inside \(T\). Efficiency makes those shares sum to one, so each player in \(T\) gets \(1/|T|\). The additivity and homogeneity axioms then determine every share for \(v\). The permutation formula yields exactly these values: in \(u_T\), the marginal contribution is one precisely when the player is last among the elements of \(T\), an event of probability \(1/|T|\). This proves existence and uniqueness under the axioms. For two features the argument gives \[\phi_1=\tfrac12(v(\{1\})-v(\varnothing))+\tfrac12(v(\{1,2\})-v(\{2\})).\] A symmetric interaction visible only when both features are present is divided in half. The definition of \(v(S)\) determines which interaction is being explained: averaging missing features independently and taking a conditional expectation can produce different coalition values. ChallengeFor \(F(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2 x_2\), compare Integrated Gradients and baseline Shapley at \((2,3)\) relative to \((0,0)\). Explain the discrepancy. Show solution Along \((2t,3t)\) the partials are \(12t^2\) and \(4t^2\), giving Integrated Gradients \((8,4)\). The baseline game is zero unless both features are present, in which case its value is 12. Each variable is last in one of the two permutations and receives attribution 6. Along the straight path the two factors of \(x_1\) give it twice the attribution of \(x_2\). In the baseline game both features are equally necessary, and arrival order splits the payoff evenly. Both totals are 12. Second challenge. For \(F(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2x_2\), compare Integrated Gradients from zero with Shapley values from zero masking. Show solution to the second challenge On the straight path \(tx\), the first partial derivative is \(2t^2x_1x_2\) and the second is \(t^2x_1^2\). The Integrated Gradients are \((2/3,1/3)F(x)\) after integrating \(t^2\) from zero to one. Under zero masking neither feature alone yields any value and the two-feature coalition yields \(F(x)\), so Shapley gives \((1/2,1/2)F(x)\). Both satisfy completeness, with different allocations of the interaction because one measures increments along a continuous path and the other averages discrete coalition orders. SourcesYang Yuan, Machine Learning, Lecture 14 from the archived slides. LIME, Integrated Gradients, and SHAP. Previous lecture · Course notes

title: ML 13: Hyperparameter Optimization and Resource Allocation
summary: Derive Gaussian-process posteriors, Expected Improvement, and hypergradients, then compare resource allocation under successive halving.
body:
Derive Gaussian-process posteriors, Expected Improvement, and hypergradients, then compare resource allocation under successive halving. The synthetic example picks the unobserved location that maximizes Expected Improvement for a minimization problem. Training and model selectionThe inner procedure produces weights \(w_T(\lambda)\) for hyperparameters \(\lambda\). The outer optimization minimizes \(F(\lambda)=L_{m val}(w_T(\lambda),\lambda)\). Fixed training time and full convergence can rank configurations differently. Random seeds make single runs noisy, so comparisons can use common seeds or repeated runs. Keep the final test set separate from the choice of hyperparameters. A grid with \(m\) values per dimension uses \(m^d\) evaluations. If one coordinate dominates, it tests just \(m\) distinct values for that coordinate. Sampling \(m^d\) configurations from a continuous distribution generally tests a different value each time along that coordinate. Distributions on positive scales that span orders of magnitude are often defined in log space. Gaussian-process predictionLet \(F\sim\mathcal{GP}(m,k)\) and observe \(y_j=F(\lambda_j)+e_j\), where independent \(e_j\sim N(0,\sigma_n^2)\). Define \(K_{ij}=k(\lambda_i,\lambda_j)\), \(\Sigma=K+\sigma_n^2I\), and \(k_\star=(k(\lambda_i,\lambda_\star))_i\). Consider the residual \[r=F(\lambda_\star)-m(\lambda_\star)-k_\star^	op\Sigma^{-1}(y-m_\Lambda).\] Its covariance with \(y\) is zero. Joint Gaussianity then makes it independent of \(y\). Its variance is obtained by expanding the squared residual. This proves the conditional mean and variance \[\mu_\star=m(\lambda_\star)+k_\star^	op\Sigma^{-1}(y-m_\Lambda),\qquad s_\star^2=k(\lambda_\star,\lambda_\star)-k_\star^	op\Sigma^{-1}k_\star.\] To predict a future noisy observation, add \(\sigma_n^2\) to the latent variance. Expected ImprovementFor a reference value \(b\) to beat in minimization, define \(\mathrm{EI}=\mathbb E[(b-F)_+]\). Write \(F=\mu+s Z\) for standard normal \(Z\), and set \(z=(b-\mu)/s\). The integral is \[\mathrm{EI}=\int_{-\infty}^z(b-\mu-su)\phi(u)\,du =(b-\mu)\Phi(z)+s\phi(z),\] because \(\phi'(u)=-u\phi(u)\). When \(s=0\), the limit is \((b-\mu)_+\). Low mean and high uncertainty can both make a point worth evaluating. Noisy evaluations may favor basing \(b\) on predicted latent values. title: ML 12: Robust Learning and Randomized Smoothing
summary: Derive exact robust margins for linear classifiers and prove a Gaussian-smoothing certificate for bounded input changes.
body:
Derive exact robust margins for linear classifiers and prove a Gaussian-smoothing certificate for bounded input changes. A shift in the input changes the probability assigned to either side of the classifier’s decision boundary. Robust risk and the envelope derivativeA perturbation set \(\Delta\) models allowable input changes. The worst-case training objective is \[\min_	heta\mathbb E_{X,Y}\!\left[\max_{\delta\in\Delta}\ell(f_	heta(X+\delta),Y)ight].\] An \(\ell_\infty\) ball bounds each coordinate change, whereas an \(\ell_2\) ball bounds total squared magnitude. abla_	heta g\) continuous. Write \(M(	heta)\) for its set of maximizers. For any \(z\in M(	heta)\), evaluating it at \(	heta+tv\) gives the lower bound \(\liminf_{t\downarrow0}(F(	heta+tv)-F(	heta))/t\ge 
abla_	heta g(	heta,z)^	op v\). For the upper bound choose a maximizer \(z_t\) at \(	heta+tv\). Since \(F(	heta)\ge g(	heta,z_t)\), the difference quotient is bounded above by the directional change in \(g\) at \(z_t\). Compactness gives a convergent subsequence of maximizers, continuity puts its limit in \(M(	heta)\), and the uniform first-order remainder yields \[F'(	heta;v)=\max_{z\in M(	heta)}
abla_	heta g(	heta,z)^	op v.\] With a unique maximizer this gives the gradient through the outer parameters. A numerical lower bound on the maximum loss can reveal failures, while a certificate needs an upper bound on the maximum or a direct invariance argument. The dual-norm identity gives \[\min_{\|\delta\|_p\le r}y(w^	op(x+\delta)+b)=m-r\|w\|_q,\quad 1/p+1/q=1.\] Hölder’s inequality gives the lower bound, and compactness of the unit ball and the definition of the dual norm give equality. The whole closed ball is classified correctly when \(m>r\|w\|_q\). At \(p=2\) the limiting radius agrees with the geometric distance from the SVM lecture. The Gaussian smoothing proofFor base classifier \(f\), smooth by class probabilities \(p_c(x)=P(f(x+Z)=c)\) with \(Z\sim N(0,\sigma^2 I)\) and choose the most likely class. Suppose the leading class \(A\) has probability at least \(\underline p_A\) at \(x\) and any other class has probability at most \(\overline p_B<\underline p_A\). Let \(P=N(x,\sigma^2I)\), \(Q=N(x+\delta,\sigma^2I)\) and \(L(z)=dQ/dP(z)\). Given fixed \(P\)-mass, a set of low likelihood ratio minimizes \(Q\)-mass. To prove it, choose \(H=\{L\le c\}\) with the desired mass, and compare any set \(E\) of equal mass: \[Q(E)-Q(H)=\int (\mathbf1_E-\mathbf1_H)(L-c)\,dP\ge0.\] Both products on the symmetric difference are nonnegative. Consequently the extremal sets are halfspaces in that direction. Projection onto \(\delta/\|\delta\|\) shifts the mean by \(\|\delta\|\) and preserves standard deviation \(\sigma\). For any class \(A\) event with the stated lower bound, its \(Q\)-mass is at least \[\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\underline p_A)-\|\delta\|/\sigma),\] and every other class has \(Q\)-mass at most \(\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\overline p_B)+\|\delta\|/\sigma)\). Therefore the prediction is unchanged for \[\|\delta\|< rac{\sigma}{2} ig(\Phi^{-1}(\underline p_A)-\Phi^{-1}(\overline p_B) ig).\] The guarantee applies to the smoothed classifier. If probabilities are estimated by sampling, substitute simultaneous valid confidence bounds into the formula. A larger \(\sigma\) increases the prefactor but may shrink the class-probability gap. ChallengeFor a binary halfspace base classifier with nonzero normal \(w\) and a point at positive signed geometric distance \(d\), derive its smoothed probability and show that the certified radius is exact. Show solution Gaussian projection along \(w/\|w\|\) has variance \(\sigma^2\), so the smoothed positive probability is \(\Phi(d/\sigma)\) and the negative probability is \(\Phi(-d/\sigma)\). The certificate radius is \(\sigma(\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(d/\sigma))-\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(-d/\sigma)))/2=d\). Smoothing leaves this halfspace’s decision boundary in place, because positive probability exceeds \(1/2\) precisely on its positive side. A shift along the negative normal of magnitude greater than \(d\) therefore switches the prediction. Second challenge. e0\). With isotropic Gaussian noise, the positive class probability at \(x\) is \(p=\Phi((w^	op x-b)/(\sigma\|w\|))\). The runner-up has probability \(1-p\), so on the positive side the certificate is \(\sigma\Phi^{-1}(p)=(w^	op x-b)/\|w\|\). Moving against the unit normal reaches the hyperplane at exactly this distance. The averaged classifier retains the original boundary. A two-dimensional query and key rotate at a shared frequency. Their relative angle changes by the difference of the position rotations. High-similarity negative examples receive a larger repulsive derivative. The actual encoder gradient couples many pairs through shared parameters. e i}e^{s_{ik}/	au}\). The graph energy accounts for the attraction term. Deriving InfoNCE from the graph cross-entropyFor each directed edge from \(i\) to \(j\), let \(w_{ij}\) be its nonnegative score and exclude self-edges. Impose the constraint that every row selects one outgoing edge. A graph is then determined by its choices \(j(i)\), and its unnormalized probability is \(\prod_i w_{i,j(i)}\). Since the constraint on one row is independent of the other rows, summing this product over all graphs gives \(\prod_i\sum_{k

e i}\exp(z_i^	op z_k/	au)}.\] This is the sum of per-anchor InfoNCE objectives, averaged over each anchor’s positives. For low-dimensional coordinates let \(w_{ij}=(1+\|y_i-y_j\|^2)^{-1}\) and \(q_{ij}=w_{ij}/Z\), \(Z=\sum_{a
e b}w_{ab}\). Self-pairs have probability zero. The heavy tail leaves room for moderate and large distances and reduces crowding in the embedding. To differentiate \(D_{m KL}(P\|Q)\), omit the constant \(\sum p_{ij}\log p_{ij}\) and write the remainder as \(\log Z-\sum p_{ij}\log w_{ij}\). For \(j
e i\), \(

e i}(p_{ij}-q_{ij})w_{ij}(y_i-y_j).\] A pair with \(p_{ij}>q_{ij}\) attracts under gradient descent. Distances between clusters and relative cluster areas can vary considerably with the initialization and perplexity. Here \(R(\alpha)\) is the rotation with rows \((\cos\alpha,-\sin\alpha)\) and \((\sin\alpha,\cos\alpha)\). Since \(R(\alpha)^	op=R(-\alpha)\) and \(R(a)R(b)=R(a+b)\), \[(R(m	heta_j)q)^	op R(n	heta_j)k=q^	op R((n-m)	heta_j)k.\] Thus the positional action on the dot product is a function of the relative position. title: ML 10: K-means and Spectral Clustering
summary: Derive Lloyd’s updates, prove the graph Laplacian’s spectral properties, and obtain a clustering algorithm by relaxing RatioCut.
body: Derive Lloyd’s updates, prove the graph Laplacian’s spectral properties, and obtain a clustering algorithm by relaxing RatioCut. The bridge is weak relative to the triangle edges. The second eigenvector places the two triangles on opposite sides of zero. Lloyd’s alternating updatesK-means minimizes \(\sum_i\|x_i-\mu_{c_i}\|^2\) over assignments and centers. With centers fixed, each point chooses its closest center independently. For a fixed nonempty cluster \(S\), expansion about its mean gives \[\sum_{i\in S}\|x_i-\mu\|^2 =\sum_{i\in S}\|x_i-\bar x_S\|^2+|S|\|\mu-\bar x_S\|^2.\] The cross term vanishes because the centered points sum to zero. Therefore the optimal center is the cluster mean. Exact alternating updates cannot increase the objective. If assignments change only on strict improvements and empty centers are held fixed, the finite number of partitions ensures eventual stability. The solution can depend on initialization. In Euclidean space, nearest centers induce convex Voronoi cells, which need not follow a curved cluster. Graph Laplacian energy and null spaceLet \(W\) be a symmetric nonnegative weight matrix, \(D_{ii}=\sum_jW_{ij}\), and \(L=D-W\). Symmetry gives \[u^\top Lu=\sum_iD_{ii}u_i^2-\sum_{ij}W_{ij}u_iu_j =\tfrac12\sum_{ij}W_{ij}(u_i-u_j)^2.\] Thus \(L\) is positive semidefinite. The energy is zero exactly when every edge of positive weight joins two equal coordinates. This means \(u\) is constant on each connected component, so the multiplicity of eigenvalue zero is the number of components. In particular, \(L\mathbf1=0\). RatioCut as a relaxationDefine \(W(A,B)=\sum_{i\in A,j\in B}W_{ij}\). For a partition \(A,B\), take \(u_i=\sqrt{|B|/(n|A|)}\) on \(A\) and \(u_i=-\sqrt{|A|/(n|B|)}\) on \(B\). Then \(\|u\|=1\) and \(u\perp\mathbf1\). All internal edges have zero energy. A crossing edge contributes its weight times \((1/|A|+1/|B|)\), so \(u^\top Lu=\operatorname{RatioCut}(A,B)\). Removing the two-level constraint permits any unit vector perpendicular to \(\mathbf1\). Expand in an eigenbasis with \(\mathbf1/\sqrt n\) first. The minimum is \(\lambda_2(L)\), achieved by a Fiedler vector, and is a lower bound on the discrete optimum. A threshold or one-dimensional two-means converts its real coordinates into a cut. For \(k\) nonempty groups, set \(H_{ij}=\mathbf1\{i\in A_j\}/\sqrt{|A_j|}\). Then \(H^\top H=I\) and \[\operatorname{tr}(H^\top LH)=\sum_j\frac{W(A_j,\overline{A_j})}{|A_j|}.\] To solve the relaxation over all \(H^\top H=I\), let \(u_i\) be Laplacian eigenvectors and write the trace as \(\sum_i\lambda_i c_i\) where \(c_i=\|H^\top u_i\|^2\). Since \(HH^\top\) is a rank-\(k\) orthogonal projector, \(0\le c_i\le1\) and \(\sum_i c_i=k\). Moving weight from a larger eigenvalue to a smaller one until the smallest \(k\) have weight one gives the lower bound \(\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i\). Taking their eigenvectors as columns attains it. This is the trace minimization proof used for the spectral embedding; each row is a node’s embedding, and k-means rounds the points to clusters. The same trace argument, applied to the largest eigenvalues, gives the PCA characterization from Lecture 9. Replacing the size of a group by its total degree gives normalized cut. Its relaxed matrix on positive-degree vertices is \(I-D^{-1/2}WD^{-1/2}\), obtained by substituting \(D^{1/2}u\) into a Rayleigh quotient with denominator \(u^\top Du\). Neighborhood definition and edge weights determine the graph; their scale affects both connectedness and the distinction between weak and strong edges. The Birkhoff proof in the lectureComplete \(H\) to an orthogonal basis and express its columns in an eigenbasis of \(L\), obtaining an orthogonal matrix \(Q\). The matrix \(B\) with entries \(Q_{ij}^2\) is doubly stochastic because each row and column of \(Q\) has squared norm one. By Birkhoff’s theorem, \(B\) is a convex combination of permutation matrices. The objective is the linear expression \(\sum_i\lambda_i\sum_{j\le k}B_{ij}\). At each permutation this is the sum of some \(k\) distinct eigenvalues, at least \(\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k\). The same is true of their convex combination. The first \(k\) eigenvectors give equality. Two supplementary proofs of the trace minimumPCA and best low-rank approximation. Choose \(c>\lambda_{\max}(L)\) and set \(A=cI-L=XX^\top\) using the symmetric square root. Minimizing \(\operatorname{tr}(H^\top LH)\) over \(H^\top H=I_k\) is equivalent to maximizing \(\operatorname{tr}(H^\top XX^\top H)\), since their sum is \(ck\). For a fixed column subspace, the best approximation of \(X\) in that subspace is the projection \(HH^\top X\). Its squared error is \(\|X\|_F^2-\operatorname{tr}(H^\top XX^\top H)\). Every matrix of rank at most \(k\) has columns in such a subspace, so the problem is exactly best rank-\(k\) approximation. Here is the singular value argument from Zeyang Zhang’s supplement. For \(n\)-column matrices \(B,C\), take the subspaces orthogonal to the leading \(i-1\) right singular vectors of \(B\) and leading \(j-1\) of \(C\). Their intersection has dimension at least \(n-i-j+2\), and \(\|(B+C)v\|\le(\sigma_i(B)+\sigma_j(C))\|v\|\) there. The variational formula for singular values, which minimizes the maximal stretch over subspaces of this dimension, gives \(\sigma_{i+j-1}(B+C)\le\sigma_i(B)+\sigma_j(C)\). This variational formula follows by choosing the trailing right singular vectors for the upper bound and intersecting any candidate subspace with the span of the first \(i+j-1\) right singular vectors for the lower bound. Set \(B=X-M\), \(C=M\), and \(j=k+1\). Since \(\sigma_{k+1}(M)=0\) for rank at most \(k\), summing squares gives \[\|X-M\|_F^2=\sum_i\sigma_i(X-M)^2\ge\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i(X)^2.\] The rank-\(k\) truncated singular value decomposition attains the bound. The largest eigenvalues of \(XX^\top=cI-L\) correspond to the smallest ones of \(L\), giving the desired trace minimum. Lagrange multipliers and the determinant argument. This follows Wenjie Huang’s supplement. For any symmetric \(A\), use the Lagrangian \(\operatorname{tr}(H^\top AH)-\operatorname{tr}(M(H^\top H-I))\), with \(M\) symmetric. The derivative of the constraint is onto the symmetric \(k\times k\) matrices, because the perturbation \(HS/2\) gives derivative \(S\) for any symmetric \(S\). Thus at a minimizer \(AH=HM\). To see the determinant step, form the block matrix \(D\) with commuting entries \(D_{ij}=\delta_{ij}A-M_{ij}I\). The cofactor identity \(\operatorname{adj}(D)D=\det(D)I\) holds over the commutative ring generated by \(A\) and \(I\): an off-diagonal entry is the expansion of a determinant with two equal columns and vanishes. Applying it to the column vectors of \(H\) gives \(p(A)h_j=0\) with \(p(t)=\det(tI_k-M)\). For simple spectrum, \(p(A)\) has at least \(k\) linearly independent null vectors, so \(p(t)\) vanishes at \(k\) distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_{i_1},\ldots,\lambda_{i_k}\) of \(A\). Since \(p\) is monic of degree \(k\), comparing the coefficient of \(t^{k-1}\) gives \(\operatorname{tr}(M)=\sum_{j=1}^k\lambda_{i_j}\). The objective is \(\operatorname{tr}(M)\) at the stationary point and is at least the sum of the smallest \(k\) eigenvalues. Choosing their eigenvectors attains equality. For repeated eigenvalues diagonalize \(M=Q\Lambda Q^\top\): \(AHQ=HQ\Lambda\), so the \(k\) orthonormal columns select eigenvalues with multiplicity at most their eigenspace dimensions. The same lower bound follows. Compactness of \(H^\top H=I\) ensures the minimum is attained. ChallengeSuppose \(G\) has exactly \(k\) connected components. Show that k-means on the rows of any orthonormal basis of the bottom-\(k\) eigenspace has a unique zero-loss grouping up to label order. Show solution The normalized component indicators form an orthonormal basis \(B\) of the null space. Every other orthonormal basis is \(BQ\) for an orthogonal \(Q\). The rows of \(B\) are constant within each component, and different components use nonzero multiples of distinct standard basis vectors, so have distinct rows. Orthogonal rotation preserves these distances. There are exactly \(k\) distinct embedded points. A zero-loss solution requires all rows assigned to a center to be identical, so its \(k\) centers must be the \(k\) distinct points and recover the components. Second challenge. For a connected weighted graph, show the normalized Laplacian has spectrum in \([0,2]\). When does the largest eigenvalue reach 2? Show solution to the second challenge For \(v=D^{-1/2}u\), the energy is \(\tfrac12\sum_{ij}W_{ij}(v_i-v_j)^2\). The bound \((a-b)^2\le2(a^2+b^2)\) makes it at most \(2\sum_iD_{ii}v_i^2=2\|u\|^2\). Equality requires \(v_i=-v_j\) on every positive-weight edge, so a connected graph has a nonzero equality vector exactly when its edges respect a bipartition. On a bipartite graph take \(v=1\) on one side and \(-1\) on the other. SourcesYang Yuan, Machine Learning, Lecture 10 from the archived slides and its trace minimization supplements. title: ML 09: PCA, Nearest Neighbors, and Metric Learning
summary: Prove the equivalence of PCA’s variance and reconstruction objectives, derive locality-sensitive hashing guarantees, and learn distances from labels.
body: Prove the equivalence of PCA’s variance and reconstruction objectives, derive locality-sensitive hashing guarantees, and learn distances from labels. Each thin segment represents a reconstruction residual. Squaring and averaging its length gives the reconstruction loss of the chosen direction. PCA and orthogonal reconstructionCenter the columns of \(X=[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\in\mathbb R^{d\times n}\) and form \(C=XX^\top/n\). A unit vector \(v\) maximizes retained variance \(v^\top Cv\) exactly when it minimizes the mean squared reconstruction error. By orthogonality, \[n^{-1}\sum_i\|x_i-vv^\top x_i\|^2=\operatorname{tr}(C)-v^\top Cv.\] Writing \(v=\sum_j a_j u_j\) in the eigenbasis gives \(v^\top Cv=\sum_j\lambda_j a_j^2\) with \(\sum_j a_j^2=1\). The maximum is the largest eigenvalue. More generally, for \(k\) orthonormal columns \(V\), the retained variance is \(\sum_j\lambda_j\|V^\top u_j\|^2\). Each weight is in \([0,1]\) and their sum is \(k\), so the largest \(k\) eigenvalues give the best possible total. The omitted eigenvalues sum to the minimum residual. For \(\lambda_1>\lambda_2\) and initial \(v_0\) with nonzero first eigencoordinate, the normalized power iteration gives a vector parallel to \(C^tv_0\). Each eigencoordinate relative to the first is multiplied by \((\lambda_j/\lambda_1)^t\), establishing convergence to the leading eigendirection. Orthogonal projection away from an exactly known leading eigenvector preserves the other eigendirections, which permits orthogonal deflation. Scaling features changes the covariance geometry, so the units of the data affect the principal directions. From neighbor search to locality-sensitive hashingThe \(k\) nearest labeled examples vote in a kNN classifier. Search is the separate problem of finding candidates quickly. In the \((R,cR)\) decision version, if there is an item within \(R\) of a query, an item within \(cR\) qualifies. Every returned candidate can be checked using its actual distance. An \((R,cR,p_1,p_2)\)-sensitive hash family offers collision probability at least \(p_1\) for near points and at most \(p_2<p_1\) for far points. For Hamming distance, a uniformly chosen coordinate agrees with probability \(1-d_H(x,y)/d\). Concatenate \(k\) independent hashes so the near and far collision probabilities become at least \(p_1^k\) and at most \(p_2^k\). Then use \(L\) independent tables. A fixed near point is missed with probability at most \((1-p_1^k)^L\le e^{-Lp_1^k}\). Take \(k=\lceil\log_{1/p_2}n\rceil\) and \(L=\lceil p_1^{-k}\rceil\). Each table contributes at most one far collision in expectation, so at most \(L\) far collisions are expected across all tables. Markov bounds the probability of more than \(aL\) far collisions by \(1/a\). A budgeted scan of at least \(\lceil aL\rceil+1\) candidates guarantees a qualifying point on the event that the fixed near point appears and there are at most \(aL\) far collisions. A union bound gives success at least \(1-e^{-1}-1/a\). Hash evaluation, distance comparisons, and table space are additional costs. The number of tables is of order \(n^\rho\) for \(\rho=\log(1/p_1)/\log(1/p_2)\). A Euclidean design takes \(h(x)=\lfloor(a^\top x+b)/w\rfloor\), where \(a\sim N(0,I)\) and \(b\) is uniform in \([0,w)\). Conditional on projected distance \(t\), the fraction of offsets putting the two points in the same bucket is \((1-t/w)_+\). Since \(t\) is distributed as \(\|x-y\||Z|\) with \(Z\sim N(0,1)\), the unconditional collision rate decreases as their original distance increases. Learning a useful metricA linear representation \(Ax\) gives squared distance \((x_i-x_j)^\top A^\top A(x_i-x_j)\). Neighborhood Components Analysis (NCA) replaces a hard neighbor choice by \[p_{ij}=\frac{e^{-\|A(x_i-x_j)\|^2}}{\sum_{k\ne i}e^{-\|A(x_i-x_k)\|^2}},\quad j\ne i,\qquad p_{ii}=0.\] The expected number of correct leave-one-out predictions is \(\sum_i\sum_{j:y_j=y_i}p_{ij}\). Excluding self-neighbors ensures that training fits relationships between distinct examples. Another approach uses a triplet objective to prefer a positive neighbor over a negative one by a margin. Under a matrix metric \(M\succeq0\), a fixed triplet yields the hinge of an affine function of \(M\), hence a convex penalty in that variable. Euclidean locality-sensitive hashingFor the \(p\)-stable construction at \(p=2\), let \(a\sim N(0,I_d)\) and \(b\) be uniform on \([0,w)\), independently, and hash \(h_{a,b}(x)=\lfloor(a^\top x+b)/w\rfloor\). Conditional on projection separation \(t=|a^\top(x-z)|\), the random shift places a bin boundary between the projections with probability \(\min(1,t/w)\). This follows because a boundary lies between them for exactly \(t\) out of \(w\) shift values when \(t<w\), and at least one boundary always lies between them when \(t\ge w\). Since \(t\overset{d}{=}\|x-z\|_2|Z|\) for \(Z\sim N(0,1)\), the collision probability at distance \(r\) is \[p(r)=\mathbb E\!\left[(1-r|Z|/w)_+\right].\] For \(0\le r_1<r_2\), use the same \(|Z|\) in both expectations. The integrand for \(r_1\) is larger on the positive-probability event \(0<|Z|<w/r_2\), and never smaller. Thus the \((R,cR)\) near and far probabilities satisfy \(p(R)>p(cR)\) for \(R>0,c>1\). Why the LMNN objective is convex in the metricFix the same-class target neighbors in advance and put \(D_{ij}=(x_i-x_j)(x_i-x_j)^\top\). A positive semidefinite matrix \(M\) gives squared distance \(d_M(i,j)=\operatorname{tr}(MD_{ij})\). The large-margin nearest neighbor objective combines the sum of target-neighbor distances and a hinge penalty \(\max(0,1+d_M(i,j)-d_M(i,k))\) on differently labeled \(k\). Both distance expressions are affine in \(M\). The maximum of two affine functions is convex, sums with nonnegative weights preserve convexity, and the positive semidefinite cone is convex since each inequality \(z^\top Mz\ge0\) is linear in \(M\). Factoring \(M=T^\top T\) gives the resulting Euclidean embedding. A bounded-work query guaranteeFor a fixed query, suppose at least one data point is within \(R\). Let \(k=\lceil\log n/\log(1/p_2)\rceil\), concatenate \(k\) independent hashes per table, and let \(\rho=\log(1/p_1)/\log(1/p_2)\). A far point collides in one table with probability at most \(p_2^k\le1/n\). Linearity of expectation bounds the total number of far candidate occurrences in \(L\) tables by \(L\), whether or not collisions for different data points are independent. By Markov, more than \(4L\) far occurrences has probability at most \(1/4\). The distinguished near point collides per table with probability at least \(p_1^k\ge p_1n^{-\rho}\). Independence across tables bounds the probability of missing it by \(\exp(-Lp_1n^{-\rho})\), at most \(1/4\) when \(L\ge n^\rho\log(4)/p_1\). If both good events occur, scanning up to \(4L+1\) candidates and checking their distances must find a point within \(cR\). This succeeds with probability at least \(1/2\) by the union bound. ChallengeFind the behavior of Gaussian bucket hashing when the projected spacing parameter \(w\) is tiny compared with the original distance \(d=\|x-y\|\). Show \(P(h(x)=h(y))\sim w/(d\sqrt{2\pi})\). Show solution The density of \(t=d|Z|\) is \(\sqrt{2/\pi}\exp(-t^2/(2d^2))/d\) for \(t\ge0\). Thus \[P=\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\frac wd\int_0^1(1-u)e^{-w^2u^2/(2d^2)}\,du.\] As \(w/d\to0\), dominated convergence gives an integral tending to \(1/2\), proving the result. Second challenge. Suppose each query uses \(L\) independent tables from the proved constant-success LSH construction. How many independent copies are required to answer \(Q\) fixed queries with total failure probability at most \(\delta\)? Show solution to the second challenge For a query with a near neighbor, each fresh copy fails with probability at most \(1/2\). Trying \(r\) copies independently reduces this to \(2^{-r}\). A union bound over queries gives at most \(Q2^{-r}\) even though different queries reuse the copies. It suffices to take \(r=\lceil\log_2(Q/\delta)\rceil\). This argument assumes the queries are fixed independently of the randomized tables. SourcesYang Yuan, Machine Learning, Lecture 9 from the archived slides. Indyk and Motwani, Approximate Nearest Neighbors. Datar et al., p-stable LSH. Previous lecture · Course notes · Next lecture

title: ML 08: Decision Trees, Random Forests, and Boosting
summary: Compute a greedy tree split, derive AdaBoost’s training and margin bounds, and connect gradient boosting to functional descent.
body: Compute a greedy tree split, derive AdaBoost’s training and margin bounds, and connect gradient boosting to functional descent. The weighted post-split impurity is about 0.317, below the parent impurity of 0.480. Greedy splits and baggingFor class proportions \(p_c\), Gini impurity is \(I(p)=1-\sum_c p_c^2\), the chance of different labels in two independent draws. A split maximizes parent impurity minus the sample-count weighted impurity of its children. The illustrated root has 6 blue and 4 orange examples. Its left child has 5 blue and 1 orange, giving \(5/18\), and its right child has 1 blue and 3 orange, giving \(3/8\). The weighted child value is \((6/10)(5/18)+(4/10)(3/8)=19/60\). Each node optimizes one split. Depth limits, minimum leaf counts, and pruning control the eventual tree size. Replacing Gini by entropy gives information gain. A bootstrap sample draws \(n\) times with replacement from \(n\) cases. A specific case is absent with probability \((1-1/n)^n\to e^{-1}\), so the trees that leave it out can supply its out-of-bag prediction. A random forest also samples feature candidates at each split. For conditional prediction variance \(\sigma^2\) and pairwise correlation \(\rho\) in an ensemble model, expanding the variance of the mean over \(B\) trees gives \(\sigma^2(\rho+(1-\rho)/B)\). The correlation term survives as the number of trees increases. AdaBoost from exponential lossFor labels and weak predictions in \(\{-1,1\}\), write \(F_t=F_{t-1}+\alpha_t h_t\). At round \(t\), set \(D_t(i)\propto e^{-y_iF_{t-1}(x_i)}\) and let \(\epsilon_t\) be the error of \(h_t\) under \(D_t\). For fixed \(h_t\), adding the new learner multiplies the empirical exponential loss by \[Z_t(\alpha)=(1-\epsilon_t)e^{-\alpha}+\epsilon_t e^\alpha.\] Differentiation gives the minimum at \(\alpha_t=\tfrac12\log((1-\epsilon_t)/\epsilon_t)\) when \(0<\epsilon_t<1/2\). Substituting gives \(Z_t=2\sqrt{\epsilon_t(1-\epsilon_t)}\). The new sample weight is \(D_{t+1}(i)=D_t(i)e^{-\alpha_t y_i h_t(x_i)}/Z_t\). A perfect weak rule can terminate boosting, and error \(1/2\) gives zero coefficient. With \(F_0=0\), the empirical exponential loss after \(T\) rounds is \(\prod_t Z_t\). Misclassification implies \(y_iF_T(x_i)\le0\), and then its exponential term is at least 1. Writing \(\epsilon_t=1/2-\gamma_t\) gives \[\widehat R(\operatorname{sign}F_T)\le\prod_t\sqrt{1-4\gamma_t^2}\le e^{-2\sum_t\gamma_t^2}.\] Moreover, for the normalized margin \(m_i=y_iF_T(x_i)/\sum_t\alpha_t\), a threshold \(\theta\) gives \[\widehat P(m_i\le\theta) \le e^{\theta\sum_t\alpha_t}\prod_t Z_t =\prod_t 2\,\epsilon_t^{(1-\theta)/2}(1-\epsilon_t)^{(1+\theta)/2}.\] The first inequality is the same exponential comparison at a positive margin threshold. For a finite base class, the reason a positive margin helps generalization can be seen by sampling weak rules independently from the normalized vote weights. At any example with margin above \(\theta\), an \(N\)-rule sampled vote has error at most \(e^{-N\theta^2/2}\) by Hoeffding. Likewise a point with nonpositive margin has probability at least \(1-e^{-N\theta^2/8}\) that its sampled vote has margin at most \(\theta/2\). Apply a union bound to the at most \(|\mathcal H|^N\) sampled votes at this fixed threshold, then average over the vote sampling. Choosing \(N\) proportional to \(\log n/\theta^2\) gives a generalization gap of order \(\sqrt{(\log|\mathcal H|\log n/\theta^2+\log(1/\delta))/n}\), with universal constants. Functional gradient boostingTreat the predictions \(F(x_i)\) as coordinates. With squared loss, the negative gradient is the observed residual \(y_i-F(x_i)\). With a general differentiable loss, set \[r_i=-\left.\frac{\partial\ell(y_i,u)}{\partial u}\right|_{u=F(x_i)}.\] Fit a weak regressor to \((x_i,r_i)\), line-search its coefficient, and update the predictions. A tree fits an allowable approximation to the descent direction. If the fitted tree predicts constants on fixed leaves, the squared-loss line search can also be performed independently per leaf. A uniform margin bound, with constantsFix a margin threshold \(0<\theta\le1\). For a normalized vote \(f\), draw \(N\) independent base hypotheses from its weights, and write \(g\) for their average. When \(yf(x)\le0\), Hoeffding gives \(\Pr_g(yg(x)>\theta/2)\le a=e^{-N\theta^2/8}\). When \(yf(x)>\theta\), it gives \(\Pr_g(yg(x)\le\theta/2)\le a\). Therefore \[P(yf\le0)\le \mathbb E_g P(yg\le\theta/2)+a,\qquad \mathbb E_g P_S(yg\le\theta/2)\le P_S(yf\le\theta)+a.\] For every one of the at most \(|\mathcal H|^N\) possible ordered sampled votes, apply the one-sided Hoeffding bound to its binary thresholded loss over \(n\) independent training examples. A union bound gives, with probability at least \(1-\delta\), \(P(yg\le\theta/2)\le P_S(yg\le\theta/2)+b\) simultaneously, where \(b=\sqrt{(N\log|\mathcal H|+\log(1/\delta))/(2n)}\). The event does not depend on the vote weights. Combining the two displays yields the uniform gap \(2a+b\). For \(n\ge2\), choose \(N=\lceil4\log n/\theta^2\rceil\) so \(a\le1/\sqrt n\). This establishes the stated order for a fixed threshold. A finite grid of thresholds can be covered by allocating part of \(\delta\) to each threshold. ChallengeShow that for finite base class, the first AdaBoost round is a greedy coordinate minimization of exponential loss, and give the exact objective improvement when the selected rule has weighted error \(\epsilon\). What changes if the class contains each sign-flipped rule? Show solution For coordinate \(h\), the minimized multiplicative ratio is \(2\sqrt{\epsilon(1-\epsilon)}\) when the new coefficient is unconstrained. If coefficients may only increase, its optimum is at zero whenever \(\epsilon\ge1/2\). On \([0,1/2]\) the ratio increases with \(\epsilon\), so the best permitted coordinate is the lowest-error rule. The decrease is current loss times \(1-2\sqrt{\epsilon(1-\epsilon)}\). With a closed-under-sign-flip class, a negative coefficient on \(h\) has the same effect as a positive coefficient on \(-h\), whose weighted error is \(1-\epsilon\). Second challenge. Derive the optimal second-order score for a new tree split when leaf weights have an \(\ell_2\) penalty. Show solution to the second challenge For a leaf let \(G\) and \(H\) be the sums of sample gradients and Hessians at the current predictions. Its quadratic term is \(Gw+\tfrac12(H+\lambda)w^2\). If \(H+\lambda>0\), the minimizer is \(-G/(H+\lambda)\) and the fitted contribution is \(-G^2/(2(H+\lambda))\). Thus split gain is half the sum of the two new \(G^2/(H+\lambda)\) scores minus half the old score and minus the extra leaf penalty. A large Newton weight alone gives no guarantee of a large gain. SourcesYang Yuan, Machine Learning, Lecture 8 from the archived slides. Breiman, Random Forests. Friedman, Greedy Function Approximation. Previous lecture · Course notes · Next lecture

title: ACG 07: Ray Intersection, Acceleration, and Light Transport
summary: Ray tracing separates two questions. An intersection query finds the first surface hit along a ray. A transport calculation determines the radiance that surface sends toward the camera. Primary visibility, shad
body: Ray tracing separates two questions. An intersection query finds the first surface hit along a ray. A transport calculation determines the radiance that surface sends toward the camera. Primary visibility, shadows, and mirror reflections use the same intersection machinery with different directions and parameter intervals. Primary and secondary raysA ray is \(r(t)=o+td\), evaluated on a permitted interval. With unit direction \(d\), \(t\) is distance. For a shadow query from \(x\) to a point light at \(\ell\), choose direction \(\ell-x\) and check for an occluder strictly between \(t=0\) and \(t=1\). A closest-hit query returns the smallest permitted intersection, while an any-hit query can stop after finding an occluder. Whitted-style recursion adds mirror reflections and refractions to direct lighting. For a unit incident direction \(d\) pointing toward a surface with unit normal \(n\), reflecting flips its normal component and keeps the tangent component, yielding \(d_r=d-2(d\cdot n)n\). Snell’s law gives the transmitted direction when refraction is possible. Recursion depth bounds the workload and truncates longer paths. Diffuse interreflection involves many incident directions rather than a single secondary ray. Sphere, plane, and triangle intersectionsFor a sphere centered at \(c\) with radius \(R\), substitute \(o+td\) into \(\|r(t)-c\|^2=R^2\) and put \(m=o-c\): \[(d\cdot d)t^2+2(m\cdot d)t+(m\cdot m-R^2)=0.\] The discriminant tests for real roots. Pick the smallest root in the allowed interval, which may be the larger quadratic root when the origin is inside the sphere. For a general implicit surface \(F(x)=0\), substitution similarly reduces the search to the scalar equation \(F(o+td)=0\). For a plane through \(A\) with normal \(n\), solve \(n\cdot(o+td-A)=0\) to obtain \(t=n\cdot(A-o)/(n\cdot d)\). A zero denominator indicates a parallel ray. The numerator then determines whether the ray lies in the plane. Möller–Trumbore combines triangle plane intersection and barycentric tests. For \(e_1=B-A\) and \(e_2=C-A\), solve \[[-d\quad e_1\quad e_2] \begin{pmatrix}t\\u\\v\end{pmatrix}=o-A.\] Set \(s=o-A\), \(p=d\times e_2\), \(q=s\times e_1\), and \(D=e_1\cdot p\). Cramer’s rule gives \(u=(s\cdot p)/D\), \(v=(d\cdot q)/D\), and \(t=(e_2\cdot q)/D\). For a nonsingular system, accept only \(u,v\ge0\), \(u+v\le1\), and a parameter \(t\) within the ray interval. Acceleration structuresTo intersect an axis-aligned bounding box, solve \(b_i^-\le o_i+t d_i\le b_i^+\) for each axis with \(d_i\ne0\). The two crossing parameters have to be sorted when the direction is negative. Intersect the resulting intervals with the ray interval: \[t_{\mathrm{enter}}=\max_i t_i^-, \qquad t_{\mathrm{exit}}=\min_i t_i^+.\] When \(d_i=0\), the ray’s fixed coordinate either excludes the whole ray or imposes no additional limit. Allow a singleton interval to retain tangential intersections and zero-thickness bounds. A uniform grid stores primitive references in cells. Its DDA traversal advances to the next crossing by comparing the candidate times for each axis, updating a crossed axis by its cell width divided by the absolute direction component. A kd-tree partitions space recursively and clips the ray interval at each split. A primitive may overlap both halves. A BVH partitions primitives instead. Its child bounding boxes may overlap, but the primitive groups in a basic BVH are disjoint. PBRT, “Bounding Volume Hierarchies” Implement near-first BVH traversalA stack stores candidate nodes and their box-entry parameters. The current best hit provides a shrinking far bound. 1234567891011121314closest = no hitfar = ray.t_maxpush root if its box intersects [ray.t_min, far]while the stack is not empty: pop node, entry if entry > far: continue if node is a leaf: test its primitives against [ray.t_min, far] update closest and far for each closer hit else: intersect each child box with [ray.t_min, far] push valid children in descending entry orderreturn closest The first child popped has the nearest box entry, so its hits can prune farther boxes early. Box entry is only a lower bound. Returning immediately from the first hit leaf can be wrong when boxes overlap. For a shadow query that needs any opaque hit, an immediate return is valid. Radiometry Quantity Definition Unit Radiant flux \(\Phi\) Energy per unit time W Radiant intensity \(I\) Flux per unit solid angle W/sr Irradiance \(E\) Incoming flux per unit surface area W/m² Radiance \(L\) Flux per projected area and unit solid angle W/(m²·sr) A patch at distance \(r\) with area \(dA\) and normal angle \(\theta\) subtends \(dA\cos\theta/r^2\) at a point source facing its front. This gives irradiance \(I\cos\theta/r^2\). Integrating general incoming radiance gives \[E(x)=\int_{\Omega^+(n)} L_i(x,\omega)(n\cdot\omega)\,d\omega.\] For uniform incident radiance \(L\), write \(d\omega=\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi\). The hemisphere integral of the cosine is \(\pi\), so the irradiance is \(\pi L\). PBRT, “Radiometry” The rendering equationA BRDF \(f_r\) relates outgoing radiance to irradiance from one incoming direction. Conservation of energy bounds the directional reflected fraction, \[\int_{\Omega^+(n)} f_r(x,\omega_i,\omega_o) (n\cdot\omega_o)\,d\omega_o\le1 .\] The Lambertian function \(\rho/\pi\) integrates to \(\rho\). For an opaque reflective surface, adding emission and summing reflected contributions gives the rendering equation, \[L_o(x,\omega_o)=L_e(x,\omega_o)+ \int_{\Omega^+(n)}f_r(x,\omega_i,\omega_o) L_i(x,\omega_i)(n\cdot\omega_i)\,d\omega_i .\] Under the outward direction convention, if the ray along \(\omega_i\) reaches \(y\) first through vacuum, then \(L_i(x,\omega_i)=L_o(y,-\omega_i)\). This couples outgoing radiance at different surfaces. Path tracing estimates the integral by sampling directions. Given a sample density \(p(\omega)\) in solid-angle units, each sample contributes its integrand divided by \(p(\omega)\), assuming the density is positive wherever the integrand is nonzero. Exercises Prune a BVH without discarding the nearest hit. Child boxes intersect the ray over \([2,8]\) and \([4,6]\). The first child reports a primitive hit at \(t=7\). Can the traversal skip the second child? What if the first hit were at \(t=3\)? Answer With a hit at \(7\), the second box begins at \(4\) and may contain a closer surface. With a hit at \(3\), its lower bound \(4\) is already farther away, so the second child can be skipped. Keep the exit root. A ray starts at \((0,0,1)\) with direction \((0,0,2)\) inside a sphere of radius \(3\) at the origin. Find the valid hit and its world-space distance. Answer Solve \((1+2t)^2=9\), giving \(t=1,-2\). The forward hit is at \((0,0,3)\), two world units from the ray origin. The direction is nonunit, so the valid parameter \(1\) is not the distance. Choose a sampling measure. For a Lambertian patch with constant incoming radiance \(L\), compare one-sample estimates from cosine-weighted hemisphere sampling and uniform hemisphere sampling. Answer With \(f_r=\rho/\pi\) and \(p(\omega)=\cos\theta/\pi\), the factor of cosine cancels and every sample gives \(\rho L\). Uniform hemisphere sampling uses \(p=1/(2\pi)\) and yields \(2\rho L\cos\theta\). Since a uniform hemisphere draw has \(\cos\theta\) uniform on \([0,1]\), the latter has mean \(\rho L\) and variance \((\rho L)^2/3\). ReferenceLi Yi, Advanced Computer Graphics, Lecture 7, “Ray Tracing I,” November 4, 2026, slides 10–39 for rays and intersections, 40–100 for acceleration, and 101–136 for radiometry and transport. title: ML 07: Support Vector Machines and Kernels
summary: Derive hard- and soft-margin SVMs, use KKT conditions to recover the classifier, and prove positive semidefiniteness of the Gaussian kernel.
body: Derive hard- and soft-margin SVMs, use KKT conditions to recover the classifier, and prove positive semidefiniteness of the Gaussian kernel. The closest points lie on the dashed support hyperplanes. The full margin is twice the distance from either hyperplane to the decision boundary. From distance to a convex programFor \(f(x)=w^\top x+b\), the signed distance of a labeled point to the separating hyperplane is \(y_i f(x_i)/\|w\|\). Its formula follows by moving \(x_i\) along the unit normal until \(f\) is zero. Rescaling \((w,b)\) by a positive scalar leaves that geometric distance unchanged. On separated data, normalize \(\min_i y_if(x_i)=1\). Maximizing the minimum distance becomes \[\min_{w,b}\tfrac12\|w\|^2 \quad\text{s.t. } y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\ge1\quad\forall i.\] The supporting hyperplanes \(f=\pm1\) are \(2/\|w\|\) apart. For nonseparable data, introduce \(\xi_i\ge0\) and require \(y_if(x_i)\ge1-\xi_i\). Minimize \(\|w\|^2/2+C\sum_i\xi_i\). With \(w,b\) fixed, the best slack is \(\xi_i=(1-y_if(x_i))_+\), which yields the hinge-loss objective. Comparing with an average hinge loss plus \(\lambda\|w\|^2/2\) gives \(\lambda=1/(nC)\). Deriving the dualConsider first \(\min_{x\ge b} x^2\). For \(\alpha\ge0\), the Lagrangian \(x^2+\alpha(b-x)\) is at most \(x^2\) on the feasible set. Its infimum over all \(x\) is \(b\alpha-\alpha^2/4\), attained at \(x=\alpha/2\). Maximizing this concave function over \(\alpha\ge0\) gives \(\alpha^\star=\max(2b,0)\) and optimal value \(\max(b,0)^2\), matching the primal minimum at \(x^\star=\max(b,0)\). The KKT conditions are \(x\ge b\), \(\alpha\ge0\), \(2x=\alpha\), and \(\alpha(x-b)=0\). When \(b=0\), the constraint is active at zero even though its optimal multiplier vanishes. With inequality multipliers \(\alpha_i,\beta_i\ge0\) for the margin and slack constraints, respectively, the Lagrangian is \[\mathcal L=\tfrac12\|w\|^2+C\sum_i\xi_i+ \sum_i\alpha_i(1-\xi_i-y_i(w^\top x_i+b))-\sum_i\beta_i\xi_i.\] For feasible primal variables, the added terms are nonpositive, so \(\inf_{w,b,\xi}\mathcal L\) is a lower bound on the primal optimum. Its infimum in \(b\) and \(\xi\) is finite only if their linear coefficients vanish. Minimizing in \(w\) completes the square. These calculations give \[w=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i x_i,\qquad \sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0,\qquad C-\alpha_i-\beta_i=0.\] Substitution gives \[\max_{0\le\alpha_i\le C,\,\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0} \left\{\sum_i\alpha_i-\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j y_i y_j x_i^\top x_j\right\}.\] Soft-margin strict feasibility follows from \(w=b=0,\xi_i=2\). Hard-margin strict feasibility follows by scaling any separator by a sufficiently large factor. Slater’s condition yields strong duality in either case. For the hard-margin problem there is no slack coefficient to impose an upper bound on \(\alpha_i\). Complementary slackness gives \(\alpha_i(1-\xi_i-y_if(x_i))=0\) and \((C-\alpha_i)\xi_i=0\). Strictly outside the margin, \(\alpha_i=0\). An interior multiplier \(0<\alpha_i<C\) has zero slack and \(y_if(x_i)=1\), hence \(b=y_i-w^\top x_i\). At \(\alpha_i=C\), the point may be inside the margin or misclassified. If there are no interior multipliers, use the corresponding KKT inequalities to find the allowable interval for \(b\). Kernels and finite Gram matricesA feature map induces \(K(x,z)=\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle\). For any finite sample and real vector \(a\), the Gram matrix satisfies \[a^\top K a=\left\|\sum_i a_i\phi(x_i)\right\|^2\ge0.\] Conversely, a symmetric kernel whose every finite Gram matrix is positive semidefinite induces a feature space. Start with finitely supported formal sums of symbols \(\delta_x\), set \(\langle\delta_x,\delta_z\rangle=K(x,z)\), and extend bilinearly. Cauchy–Schwarz for this semidefinite form follows by requiring \(\|u+tv\|^2\ge0\) for all \(t\). Therefore zero-norm vectors are orthogonal to the whole space. Quotient them out, take the Hilbert completion, and map \(x\) to the equivalence class of \(\delta_x\). This construction suffices for the kernel trick. Mercer expansions additionally impose conditions on the integral operator and its domain. The SVM dual replaces dot products by \(K\). The quadratic term has matrix \(\operatorname{diag}(y)K\operatorname{diag}(y)\), which remains positive semidefinite, so the maximization remains concave. The prediction is \(f(x)=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i K(x_i,x)+b\). For \((x^\top z)^2\) on \(\mathbb R^2\), one explicit feature map is \((x_1^2,\sqrt2 x_1x_2,x_2^2)\). For the Gaussian, write \[K(x,z)=e^{-\|x\|^2/(2\sigma^2)}e^{-\|z\|^2/(2\sigma^2)} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{(x^\top z)^m}{m!\sigma^{2m}}.\] Each power is a kernel because \((x^\top z)^m=\langle x^{\otimes m},z^{\otimes m}\rangle\), including the constant kernel for \(m=0\). Partial sums have nonnegative Gram quadratic forms, and their finite-entry limits do also. Multiplying by the point factors applies the same diagonal scaling to both sides of the Gram matrix. This proves the Gaussian is a valid kernel. ChallengesProblem 1Strengthen the Gaussian proof: show its Gram matrix is positive definite for any finite set of pairwise distinct points and any finite \(\sigma>0\). Show solution If a quadratic form is zero, the preceding expansion expresses it as a sum of nonnegative squared norms. Writing \(b_i=a_i e^{-\|x_i\|^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), every tensor moment \(\sum_i b_i x_i^{\otimes m}\) must vanish. Pick a vector \(v\) such that the numbers \(s_i=v^\top x_i\) are all distinct. This is possible because the forbidden vectors lie in a finite union of proper hyperplanes. Contracting with \(v^{\otimes m}\) gives \(\sum_i b_is_i^m=0\) for \(m=0,\ldots,n-1\). The Vandermonde determinant is \(\prod_{i<j}(s_j-s_i)\ne0\), so all \(b_i\) and hence all \(a_i\) vanish. Problem 2Solve the one-dimensional soft-margin SVM for \((-1,-1)\) and \((1,1)\) at arbitrary \(C>0\). Which intercepts are optimal? Show solution The balance constraint gives \(\alpha_1=\alpha_2=\alpha\), and the dual objective is \(2\alpha-2\alpha^2\). Hence \(\alpha=\min(C,1/2)\) and \(w=2\alpha\). If \(C>1/2\), both multipliers are interior, so the margin equalities force \(b=0\). If \(C\le1/2\), the positive multipliers give \(\xi_1=1-w+b\) and \(\xi_2=1-w-b\). The feasible interval is \(|b|\le1-w\), reducing to zero at \(C=1/2\). All intercepts in the interval have the same total slack and satisfy KKT. SourcesYang Yuan, Machine Learning (2026), Lecture 7. title: ACG 06: Shading, Texture Filtering, and Shadows
summary: Shading computes the appearance of a visible sample. Its result depends on the local surface orientation, the attributes interpolated across the projected triangle, the area of the texture seen by the sample, a
body: Shading computes the appearance of a visible sample. Its result depends on the local surface orientation, the attributes interpolated across the projected triangle, the area of the texture seen by the sample, and whether the light reaches the surface. Lambert and Blinn–PhongLet \(n\) be the unit normal, \(\ell\) the direction toward the source, and \(v\) the direction toward the viewer. A patch of physical area \(dA\) presents projected area \(dA\max(0,n\cdot\ell)\) to incoming light. For a point source with radiant intensity \(I\) in the direction toward the surface and distance \(r\), the resulting irradiance is \[E=\frac I{r^2}\max(0,n\cdot\ell).\] A Lambertian surface gives a direction-independent outgoing radiance \(kE\). The total outgoing flux per surface area is \(kE\int_{\Omega^+}\cos\theta\,d\omega=\pi kE\). Therefore a diffuse reflectance \(\rho\) gives \(k=\rho/\pi\). This normalization connects the classroom cosine term to a physically defined BRDF. Blinn–Phong estimates a specular lobe via \(\max(0,n\cdot h)^p\), where \(h\) is the normalized \(\ell+v\) and the exponent \(p\) controls the lobe width. Local models can include ambient light as a constant approximation to unresolved transport. Flat shading uses one normal per face. Gouraud shading interpolates colors computed at the vertices and can miss a highlight entirely if it lies between them. Phong shading interpolates normals, renormalizes them, and evaluates lighting per fragment. Perspective-correct interpolationConsider clip positions \(c_i\) with fourth components \(w_i\) and affine weights \(\mu_i\) before projection. For the covered screen point, the perspective divide gives \[\frac{\sum_i\mu_i(c_i)_{xy}}{\sum_i\mu_iw_i} =\sum_i\frac{\mu_iw_i}{\sum_j\mu_jw_j} \frac{(c_i)_{xy}}{w_i}.\] By uniqueness of barycentric coordinates, screen weights \(\lambda_i\) are \(\mu_iw_i/\sum_j\mu_jw_j\). Solving for the original weights gives the rule for vertex attribute \(a\), \[a=\frac{\sum_i\lambda_i a_i/w_i}{\sum_i\lambda_i/w_i}.\] In a rasterizer, compute \(a_i/w_i\) and \(1/w_i\) at the vertices, interpolate both independently in screen space, then take the quotient. In texture coordinates, this produces the correct texture motion when a surface tilts relative to the camera. UV seams may duplicate a geometric vertex in the attribute buffer so adjacent triangles can use different UV values. Filtering texturesMagnification calls for reconstruction between texels. With fractional offsets \(s,t\in[0,1]\), bilinear interpolation produces \[c(s,t)=(1-t)\left[(1-s)c_{00}+sc_{10}\right] +t\left[(1-s)c_{01}+sc_{11}\right].\] Minification calls for an average across the texture footprint. A mipmap filters and halves both texture dimensions at each level. The full chain for a large square power-of-two texture approaches \(1+1/4+1/16+\cdots=4/3\) times the base storage. Select a mip level from derivativesEstimate texel-space footprint vectors from the derivatives of normalized UV coordinates. Convert normalized coordinates to texel units with the base width and height before taking vector lengths. 123456789101112from math import floor, hypot, log2def sample_trilinear(texture, uv, grad_x, grad_y): w, h = texture.base_size a = hypot(grad_x[0]*w, grad_x[1]*h) b = hypot(grad_y[0]*w, grad_y[1]*h) lod = min(log2(max(1.0, a, b)), texture.last_level) low = floor(lod) high = min(low + 1, texture.last_level) s = lod - low return ((1 - s)*texture.bilinear(low, uv) + s*texture.bilinear(high, uv)) A derivative magnitude of one texel per screen pixel uses level zero. A magnitude of eight selects level three. Averaging neighboring mip levels reduces transitions between discrete estimates. An elongated anisotropic footprint still calls for more sampling along its long axis than along its short axis. Isotropic mip selection based on the larger length can blur details across the short axis. Texture channels may also store normals, volume densities, or displacements. For a local height field \((u,v,h(u,v))\), crossing the two partial derivatives gives the normal \((-h_u,-h_v,1)\). Bump and normal mapping change the direction used for shading. Displacement moves surface positions and therefore can change the silhouette or cast shadows. Two-pass shadow mappingFirst, rasterize from the light and store the nearest depth for each sample. Then rasterize from the eye. Project each camera-visible fragment into the light’s clip coordinates, divide by its fourth component, and compare the result with the shadow depth in that light-space sample. If the query is farther by more than a tolerance, a surface lies between it and the source. Too little bias reveals artifacts from finite precision and resolution. Too much moves the shadow away from its caster. An area light requires integrating visibility over its surface; one shadow view samples only one position. Exercises Quantify interpolation drift. Triangle vertices have clip \(w=(1,2,4)\), scalar attributes \((0,1,1)\), and screen weights \((1/2,1/4,1/4)\). Calculate the correct scalar and the screen-linear error. Answer The denominator is \(1/2+1/8+1/16=11/16\). The numerator is \(1/8+1/16=3/16\), giving \(3/11\). The direct estimate is \(1/2\), an overestimate of \(5/22\). Select the filtering footprint. For a \(1024\times512\) base map, normalized derivatives along screen \(x\) and \(y\) are \((1/256,0)\) and \((0,1/64)\). Find the mip level and estimate the ratio between the two footprint axes. Answer The vectors in texel units are \((4,0)\) and \((0,8)\), so max-length mip selection yields \(\log_2 8=3\). These orthogonal footprint axes are in a ratio of \(2:1\). An isotropic level covers approximately eight texels on both axes and filters across twice the short-axis length. Compare diffuse normalization. A surface with \(\rho=0.7\) receives irradiance \(E=10\,\mathrm{W/m^2}\). Compare outgoing radiance and total flux per unit area for the expressions \(\rho E\) and \(\rho E/\pi\) interpreted as radiance. Answer The normalized radiance is \(7/\pi\,\mathrm{W/(m^2\,sr)}\) and its hemisphere integral is \(7\,\mathrm{W/m^2}\). Taking the radiance as \(7\,\mathrm{W/(m^2\,sr)}\) yields \(7\pi\,\mathrm{W/m^2}\), more than twice the incident power density. ReferenceLi Yi, Advanced Computer Graphics, Lecture 6, “Shading,” October 28, 2026, slides 5–44 for local shading, 45–95 for interpolation and texture queries, and 96–124 for texture applications and shadows.
