title: ML 06: Linear Models, Sparsity, and Compressed Sensing
summary: Derive least squares, perceptron convergence, logistic curvature, and soft thresholding, then prove when sparse signals can be recovered.
body:
Derive least squares, perceptron convergence, logistic curvature, and soft thresholding, then prove when sparse signals can be recovered. The diamond has a minimizer on a coordinate axis. The disk has a minimizer with two nonzero coordinates. Least squares and ridgeFor a design matrix \(X\) and responses \(y\), stationarity of \(\|Xw-y\|^2/2\) gives \(X^	op Xw=X^	op y\). The fitted response is the orthogonal projection of \(y\) onto \(\operatorname{col}(X)\), even when several parameter vectors attain it. Ridge adds \(\lambda\|w\|^2/2\). With \(\lambda>0\) and thin SVD \(X=U\Sigma V^	op\), \[w_\lambda=(X^	op X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^	op y =\sum_i rac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_i^2+\lambda}\langle u_i,yangle v_i.\] This follows by diagonalizing \(X^	op X\) in the right-singular basis. In a direction with small positive singular value, least squares uses a large inverse gain \(1/\sigma_i\). Ridge shrinks that gain. The normal equation is a linear system that can be solved without forming the inverse. Why the perceptron terminates on separated dataTake labels \(\pm1\), norms \(\|x_i\|\le R\), and a unit vector \(w^\star\) with \(y_i(w^\star)^	op x_i\ge\gamma>0\). Starting at zero, update \(w\gets w+y_ix_i\) on a mistake or tie. After \(M\) updates, \((w^\star)^	op w_M\ge M\gamma\) by summing the projected increments. Each update also satisfies \[\|w+y_ix_i\|^2=\|w\|^2+2y_iw^	op x_i+\|x_i\|^2\le\|w\|^2+R^2.\] Thus \(M\gamma\le\|w_M\|\le R\sqrt M\), proving \(M\le(R/\gamma)^2\). A bias is handled by augmenting the vectors with a constant feature and recomputing the radius and margin. Logistic likelihood and cross-entropyFor \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\), a Bernoulli model uses \(p_i=\sigma(s_i)\), where \(s_i=w^	op x_i\). Its negative log likelihood equals \(\log(1+e^{s_i})-y_i s_i\). Since \(\sigma'(s)=\sigma(s)(1-\sigma(s))\), \[
abla_w\ell_i=(p_i-y_i)x_i,\qquad 
abla_w^2\ell_i=p_i(1-p_i)x_ix_i^	op.\] The Hessian is positive semidefinite and bounded by \(x_ix_i^	op/4\). The loss equals cross-entropy. At a fixed input, cross-entropy between the true Bernoulli parameter \(q\) and prediction \(p\) is \(H(q)+D_{m KL}(q\|p)\), minimized at \(p=q\) by nonnegativity of KL. For separable training data the unregularized empirical loss approaches zero along a growing separating direction and has no finite minimizer. LASSO and proximal gradientWith \(X^	op X=I\), the LASSO objective \(\|Xw-y\|^2/2+\lambda\|w\|_1\) separates into \(	frac12(u-z)^2+\lambda|u|\) with \(z=(X^	op y)_j\). Stationarity gives \(u=z-\lambda\) when \(u>0\) and \(u=z+\lambda\) when \(u<0\). At zero, the subgradient interval contains zero exactly when \(|z|\le\lambda\). Therefore \[S_\lambda(z)=\operatorname{sign}(z)(|z|-\lambda)_+.\] For general \(X\), minimize the first-order loss model plus a quadratic proximity penalty and the \(\ell_1\) term. Completing the square gives the proximal update \(w^+=S_{\eta\lambda}(w-\eta X^	op(Xw-y))\) coordinatewise. The same threshold determines which coordinates become exactly zero. Sparse recovery and restricted geometryFrom measurements \(y=Aw\), basis pursuit solves \(\min_z\|z\|_1\) subject to \(Az=y\). Uniform unique recovery of every \(s\)-sparse \(w\) is equivalent to the null-space property \[\|h_S\|_1<\|h_{S^c}\|_1\qquad(0
e h\in\ker A,\ |S|\le s).\] Sufficiency follows from \(\|w+h\|_1\ge\|w\|_1-\|h_S\|_1+\|h_{S^c}\|_1>\|w\|_1\) for \(S=\operatorname{supp}(w)\). If the inequality fails, take \(w=-h_S\) and competitor \(h_{S^c}=w+h\). Both have the same measurements and the competitor has norm no greater. The order-\(k\) restricted isometry property (RIP) asks that \((1-\delta_k)\|z\|^2\le\|Az\|^2\le(1+\delta_k)\|z\|^2\) for every \(k\)-sparse vector. The difference of two \(s\)-sparse candidates is \(2s\)-sparse. If both have residual at most \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta_{2s}<1\), their distance is at most \(2\varepsilon/\sqrt{1-\delta_{2s}}\) by the lower RIP inequality and the triangle inequality. Exact measurements give uniqueness within the sparse class. This argument concerns sparse candidates. A basis-pursuit guarantee needs to control differences that may be dense. Why the order-\(2s\) RIP can recover dense but compressible signalsSuppose \(A\) has order-\(2s\) RIP constant \(\delta<1/(1+\sqrt2)\) and \(\hat x\) solves basis pursuit from \(Ax\). Let \(h=\hat x-x\), and let \(S_0\) index the \(s\) largest coordinates of \(x\) in magnitude. Since \(\|\hat x\|_1\le\|x\|_1\), the triangle inequality on \(S_0\) and its complement gives \[\|h_{S_0^c}\|_1\le\|h_{S_0}\|_1+2\|x_{S_0^c}\|_1.\] Break \(S_0^c\) into blocks \(S_1,S_2,\ldots\) of size \(s\) in decreasing order of \(|h_i|\), except possibly the final block. Each entry in \(S_j\) is bounded by the average absolute entry in \(S_{j-1}\) for \(j\ge2\), so \(\sum_{j\ge2}\|h_{S_j}\|\le\|h_{S_0^c}\|_1/\sqrt s\). For disjointly supported \(s\)-sparse vectors \(u,v\), polarize the measured squared norms of the sum and difference of their unit normalizations. The RIP bounds their measured inner product by \(|\langle Au,Avangle|\le\delta\|u\|\|v\|\). Set \(H=S_0\cup S_1\). Because \(Ah=0\), \(\|Ah_H\|^2=-\sum_{j\ge2}\langle Ah_H,Ah_{S_j}angle\). Split \(h_H\) into its two blocks to apply the inner-product bound: \[(1-\delta)\|h_H\|^2 \le\sqrt2\delta\|h_H\|\sum_{j\ge2}\|h_{S_j}\|.\] With \(ho=\sqrt2\delta/(1-\delta)<1\) and \(\sigma=\|x_{S_0^c}\|_1/\sqrt s\), these estimates give \(\|h_H\|\leho(\|h_H\|+2\sigma)\) and hence \(\|h_H\|\le2ho\sigma/(1-ho)\). Finally \(\|h\|\le\|h_H\|+\sum_{j\ge2}\|h_{S_j}\|\le2\|h_H\|+2\sigma\), so \[\|\hat x-x\|_2\le rac{2(1+ho)}{1-ho} rac{\|x_{S_0^c}\|_1}{\sqrt s}.\] The right-hand side vanishes for an \(s\)-sparse signal. With measured noise the equality \(Ah=0\) is replaced by a residual bound and contributes an additional error term. Why Gaussian measurements workFor Gaussian measurements with entries distributed as \(N(0,1/m)\), a fixed unit vector has squared measured norm distributed as \(\chi^2_m/m\). Its deviation outside \(1\pm t\) has probability at most \(2e^{-cmt^2}\) for \(0<t<1\), from the moment-generating function of \(\chi^2_m\). On one support of size \(k\), take a \(1/4\)-net of the unit sphere with at most \(9^k\) points by a disjoint-ball volume argument. For \(B=A_S^	op A_S-I\), if all net values satisfy \(|v^	op Bv|\le\delta/2\), then \(\|B\|\le\delta\): approximate a maximizing unit vector by a net vector and bound the quadratic-form difference by \(2\|B\|/4\). A union bound over supports and net points gives the order \(m\gtrsim\delta^{-2}k\log(ed/k)\) for constant failure probability. For a known sparse basis use \(A\Psi\). For a nonlinear generator \(G\), the analogous geometric condition controls lengths of secants \(G(u)-G(v)\), which addresses identifiability even when optimizing over \(u\) remains difficult. For a fixed orthogonal basis \(\Psi\), the transpose of each row of \(A\Psi\) is a linear transform of a jointly Gaussian vector, with covariance \(\Psi^	op(I/m)\Psi=I/m\). Zero covariance gives independence for Gaussian coordinates, and the rows remain independent. Thus \(A\Psi\) has the same law as \(A\), giving the same high-probability guarantee for signals sparse in that basis. Recovery with a nonlinear generatorLet \(S=\{G(z):z\in\mathbb R^k\}\) and \(y=Ax^\star+\eta\). Suppose \(A\) has a lower secant bound \(\|A(u-v)\|\ge(2/3)\|u-v\|\) for all \(u,v\in S\). Choose a nearest comparator \(u\) in the closure of \(S\), which exists because the distance to \(x^\star\) has bounded sublevel sets. The secant and residual inequalities extend to the closure by continuity. For this fixed comparator, suppose \(\|A(u-x^\star)\|\le(5/3)\|u-x^\star\|\). If \(\hat x=G(\hat z)\) has measured residual within \(\varepsilon\) of the infimum, then \[	frac23\|\hat x-u\| \le\|A(\hat x-u)\| \le2\|A(u-x^\star)\|+2\|\eta\|+\varepsilon.\] Divide by \(2/3\) and add \(\|u-x^\star\|\) to obtain a reconstruction error at most \(6\inf_z\|G(z)-x^\star\|+3\|\eta\|+2\varepsilon\). For a fixed depth-\(D\) ReLU generator of layer width at most \(c\), the Gaussian sample bound is order \(kD\log c\). Each feasible activation pattern gives an affine output on the corresponding latent region. A layer cuts such a region by at most \(c\) hyperplanes in \(\mathbb R^k\), creating at most \(\sum_{j=0}^k{c\choose j}\) pieces (add one hyperplane and count its induced regions inductively). Across all layers the number of pieces is at most \((c+1)^{O(kD)}\). Secants lie in a union of subspaces of dimension at most \(2k+1\), one for each pair of affine images. Apply Gaussian concentration and the net argument to each and union bound. This yields the lower secant inequality with probability \(1-e^{-\Omega(m)}\) for sufficiently many measurements. The upper comparator bound also follows from fixed-vector concentration. The argument assumes approximate minimization of the measured residual and keeps that error explicit. ChallengesProblem 1Suppose all columns of \(A\) have unit Euclidean norm and mutual coherence \(\mu=\max_{i
e j}|a_i^	op a_j|\). Prove basis pursuit recovers every \(s\)-sparse vector if \((2s-1)\mu<1\). Show solution For \(h\in\ker A\), take the inner product of \(\sum_jh_ja_j=0\) with \(a_i\). This gives \(|h_i|\le\mu\sum_{j
e i}|h_j|\), hence \((1+\mu)|h_i|\le\mu\|h\|_1\). Sum over any \(S\) of size at most \(s\) to obtain \(\|h_S\|_1\le s\mu\|h\|_1/(1+\mu)<\|h\|_1/2\). This is exactly the strict null-space inequality for nonzero \(h\). Problem 2For least squares penalized by \(\lambda_1\|w\|_1+\lambda_2\|w\|^2/2\), derive the solution when \(X^	op X=I\). Prove uniqueness for arbitrary \(X\) when \(\lambda_2>0\). Show solution Put \(z=X^	op y\). Each coordinate minimizes \((1+\lambda_2)u^2/2-z_ju+\lambda_1|u|\), giving \(S_{\lambda_1}(z_j)/(1+\lambda_2)\) by its three subgradient cases. For arbitrary \(X\), the quadratic Hessian obeys \(X^	op X+\lambda_2I\succeq\lambda_2I\). Adding the convex penalty preserves strong convexity, and coercivity gives existence, hence the minimizer is unique. SourcesYang Yuan, Machine Learning (2026), Lecture 6 and Problem Set 4. title: ACG 05: Rasterization, Sampling, and Visibility
summary: Rasterization converts projected geometry into samples on a finite grid. Triangle edge tests decide which samples are covered, filtering limits aliasing, and the depth buffer resolves opaque visibility at each
body:
Rasterization converts projected geometry into samples on a finite grid. Triangle edge tests decide which samples are covered, filtering limits aliasing, and the depth buffer resolves opaque visibility at each sample. Sampling a projected triangleA pixel indexed by \((i,j)\) can be represented by the square \([i,i+1]	imes[j,j+1]\). Center sampling tests the continuous triangle at \((i+	frac12,j+	frac12)\). A covered sample initially says nothing about the rest of the pixel. A triangle can cross a pixel without touching its center. For counterclockwise vertices \(A,B,C\) in a coordinate system with \(y\) pointing upward, use the directed edge function \[E_{AB}(P)=(B_x-A_x)(P_y-A_y)-(B_y-A_y)(P_x-A_x).\] The function is a signed area scaled by two. The inside of a counterclockwise triangle lies to the left of all three oriented edges. Equivalently, \(E_{AB}(P)/E_{AB}(C)\) is the barycentric weight for \(C\), and the other two come from cyclic permutations. The three nonnegative weights sum to one and give a convex combination of the vertices. Incremental edge evaluationFor fixed vertices, \(E(x,y)\) is affine. Moving one coordinate unit to the right changes it by \(-(B_y-A_y)\), and moving up changes it by \(B_x-A_x\). Initialize once at the first sample center of the triangle’s bounding box, cache a row start for each edge, and step across the row by addition. With an integer grid of \(S\) subpixel units per pixel, the increments for one pixel are \(-S(B_y-A_y)\) horizontally and \(S(B_x-A_x)\) vertically. Choose even \(S\) so pixel centers are representable and quantize shared vertices consistently. 1234567for each scanline y in the bounding box: e0, e1, e2 = saved values at the first pixel center for each x in the scanline: if all three edges accept their current values: emit the covered sample with barycentric weights e0, e1, e2 += horizontal increments saved values += vertical increments In this \(y\)-up, counterclockwise convention, accept equality on an edge with \(B_y<A_y\), or on a horizontal edge with \(B_x<A_x\). A reversed shared edge has exactly the opposite tie classification. This fills the left and top boundaries consistently and leaves the bottom and right boundaries for their neighbors. With \(y\) pointing down, derive the rule again from the winding convention. A tile can be rejected when the maximum of an edge function over its four corners fails that edge test. Why sampling aliases frequenciesSampling step \(T\) is equivalent to multiplying by \(\sum_k\delta(t-kT)\). With the Fourier convention \(S(
u)=\int s(t)e^{-2\pi i
u t}dt\), the impulse train transforms into another impulse train at intervals \(1/T\) with nonzero weight \(1/T\). Multiplication in time becomes convolution in frequency, so \[S_s(
u)= rac1T\sum_k S\left(
u- rac{k}{T}ight).\] A band-limited signal with bandwidth \(B\) avoids overlap when \(1/T>2B\). Otherwise, distinct spectra may produce the same samples. The cosines at frequencies \(
u\) and \(m/T-
u\) agree at all sample times by periodicity and even symmetry. A triangle boundary creates a discontinuity, which has high-frequency content beyond any finite sample rate. Jagged edges and the apparent reversal of a filmed wheel are spatial and temporal examples of aliasing. Prefiltering and multisamplingAn ideal box average for a pixel region \(A\) and triangle \(T_	riangle\) is \[c_A= rac1{|A|}\int_A\mathbf 1_{T_	riangle}(x,y)\,dx\,dy = rac{|A\cap T_	riangle|}{|A|}.\] A constant foreground and a constant background can be blended in linear color space according to this coverage. With independent uniform subsamples, their average estimates \(c_A\) without bias, with variance \(c_A(1-c_A)/N\). A regular subsample grid is deterministic quadrature, so its error depends on alignment with the edge. MSAA stores several coverage and depth samples while letting a shaded value serve multiple covered samples. It can smooth triangle edges without shading every subsample independently. High-frequency shading within a triangle retains its own sampling problem and can require texture filtering or per-sample shading. Z-bufferingStart every depth sample at \(+\infty\) when smaller means nearer. Update the sample’s depth and color only if a new opaque fragment is closer. After any number of inputs, the buffer stores the minimum submitted depth: the empty minimum is \(+\infty\), and one update takes the minimum of the previous minimum and the arriving depth. This invariant gives order independence for distinct opaque depths. Equal depths depend on the comparison and submission order. A global painter’s ordering can fail when three faces cyclically occlude one another. The Z-buffer resolves visibility locally, though overdraw can require testing many fragments per sample. Transparent fragments generally require combining several contributions and cannot use nearest-depth selection alone. Reconstruction recapThe lecture first concludes its discussion of specialized reconstruction. In linear blend skinning, a bind-pose vertex \(v\) moves to \(\sum_j w_jG_j(	heta)G_j(0)^{-1}v\), where \(G_j\) is the global joint transform and the weights sum to one. At the bind pose each transform pair becomes identity, and the vertex stays fixed. To estimate the pose from one image, minimize projected joint error and regularize body shape and pose. Indoor reconstruction can estimate object shapes, placements, and room layout separately, then assemble them in one scene. Exercises Prove shared-edge ownership. Two consistently counterclockwise triangles share an edge, and a sample is in the relative interior of that edge. Why does the fill rule assign it to exactly one triangle? Answer For a sample in the relative interior of a proper shared edge the other two edge tests of each triangle are positive. On the shared edge the tests are both zero. Its directed increments \((dx,dy)\) are opposite in the two triangles. If \(dy
e0\), exactly one orientation has \(dy<0\). Otherwise \(dx
e0\) and exactly one has \(dx<0\). Only that triangle accepts equality. Compute analytic antialiasing. A triangle covers the portion of the unit pixel where \(x+y<0.75\). Compare exact coverage with center sampling and a \(2	imes2\) grid of quarter-offset samples. Answer Exact coverage is the right-triangle area \(0.75^2/2=0.28125\). The center has sum \(1\) and returns zero. The four grid sums are \(0.5,1,1,1.5\), giving estimated coverage \(0.25\). Find the alias. A signal \(\cos(2\pi\cdot 47t)\) is sampled at \(60\) Hz. Which nonnegative frequency in \([0,30]\) matches it, and can a post-sampling low-pass filter distinguish the two? Answer The aliased frequency is \(60-47=13\) Hz, since \(\cos(2\pi\cdot47k/60)=\cos(2\pi k-2\pi\cdot13k/60)\). Both continuous signals give exactly the same discrete input. A filter on that input has no evidence from which to distinguish their origins. title: ML 05: PAC Learning and VC Dimension
summary: Prove finite-class sample bounds and compute VC dimension by combining explicit realizations with impossible labelings.
body: Prove finite-class sample bounds and compute VC dimension by combining explicit realizations with impossible labelings. Opposite vertices of the square share a label. The two convex hulls intersect at its center. Realizable and agnostic PAC guaranteesIn binary classification, \(R(h)\) is the probability of error on an independent test draw. Realizable PAC learning assumes some hypothesis in the class has zero risk. The learner must output a predictor with risk at most \(\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\) over the training sample. Agnostic PAC learning permits arbitrary labels and asks for risk within \(\varepsilon\) of \(\inf_{h\in\mathcal H}R(h)\). For any fixed hypothesis of risk greater than \(\varepsilon\), the chance it makes no errors on \(n\) independent examples is \((1-R(h))^n\le e^{-n\varepsilon}\). A union bound over a finite class and the existence of a consistent hypothesis give the realizable ERM bound \[n\ge\frac{\log|\mathcal H|+\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon}.\] For the agnostic case, two-sided Hoeffding and a union bound give \[P\!\left(\sup_{h\in\mathcal H}|\widehat R(h)-R(h)|>\varepsilon/2\right) \le 2|\mathcal H|e^{-n\varepsilon^2/2}.\] On the complementary event, \(R(\widehat h)\le\widehat R(\widehat h)+\varepsilon/2\le\widehat R(h)+\varepsilon/2\le R(h)+\varepsilon\) for every \(h\). Take the infimum. A population-risk comparison with the Bayes predictor separates approximation error, \(\inf_{\mathcal H}R-R(h^\star)\), from the learner’s excess above the best in its class. For a no-free-lunch example, select labels independently and uniformly for each point in a uniform domain of \(2n\) points, then draw \(n\) training examples. At least half the domain remains unseen. Conditional on the data, each unseen label remains an independent fair coin, giving expected risk at least \(1/4\) over the labeling and sample. Some deterministic labeling attains that lower bound in expectation over training draws. A random risk in \([0,1]\) satisfies \(\mathbb E R\le 1/8+(7/8)P(R\ge1/8)\), so for that labeling the learner has risk at least \(1/8\) with probability at least \(1/7\). If \(\mathcal H\) has infinite VC dimension, we can choose a shattered \(2n\)-point set for every \(n\). Its deterministic labeling is then realizable in \(\mathcal H\), so the bound contradicts any distribution-free PAC sample complexity at, for example, \(\varepsilon=1/9,\delta=1/8\). Infinite classes can have small effective complexityFor thresholds \(h_t(x)=\mathbf1\{x\ge t\}\) on the line, two ordered points cannot receive \((1,0)\), but one point can receive either label. The VC dimension is 1. A single interval shatters two points, while three ordered points cannot receive \((1,0,1)\), so its dimension is 2. For a realizable threshold at \(t^\star\), any consistent empirical minimizer has zero sample points in its error interval. If the empirical threshold is larger than \(t^\star\), the error interval is an initial segment of \([t^\star,\infty)\); if it is smaller, the error interval is a terminal segment of \((-\infty,t^\star)\). On each side with enough mass, choose the closest fixed segment of mass at least \(\varepsilon\), using the probability quantile and including the boundary atom if needed to reach \(\varepsilon\). Every error interval on that side of mass greater than \(\varepsilon\) contains this segment. Therefore the probability of any consistent threshold with risk greater than \(\varepsilon\) is at most \(2(1-\varepsilon)^n\). This directly yields order \(\log(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) samples. The same argument applies to concentric disks by replacing \(x\) with negative distance to the known center. In \(\mathbb R^d\), an affine halfspace shatters \(d+1\) affinely independent points because an affine function interpolates arbitrary assigned values \(\pm1\). For any \(d+2\) points, the augmented vectors \((x_i,1)\) have a nontrivial linear dependence. Its coefficients sum to zero, and the positive and negative groups therefore have convex combinations representing the same point. Opposite labels on those groups cannot be realized. Thus the dimension is exactly \(d+1\). Sauer–Shelah and the generalization boundLet \(\Pi_d(n)\) denote the largest possible trace size on \(n\) points for VC dimension at most \(d\). Split the traces on the first \(n-1\) points into prefixes appearing at least once and prefixes that can be extended with either last label. The first family has VC dimension at most \(d\), and the second at most \(d-1\), because shattering \(d\) points with both extensions would shatter \(d+1\) points. Thus \(\Pi_d(n)\le\Pi_d(n-1)+\Pi_{d-1}(n-1)\). The base cases \(n=0\) and \(d=0\) have at most one trace. Pascal’s identity yields \[\Pi_{\mathcal H}(n)\le\sum_{j=0}^d {n\choose j}\le(en/d)^d\qquad(1\le d\le n).\] For the last inequality, multiply the binomial sum by \((d/n)^d\), use \((d/n)^d\le(d/n)^j\) for \(j\le d\), and bound \((1+d/n)^n\) by \(e^d\). To see why this controls uniform convergence, add an independent ghost sample of size \(n\). For \(n\varepsilon^2\ge 2\), a hypothesis whose true and empirical risk differ by more than \(\varepsilon\) has at least a constant probability that its ghost error is within \(\varepsilon/2\) of the truth, by Chebyshev’s inequality for Bernoulli averages. The resulting two-sample event has a discrepancy above \(\varepsilon/2\). Swap the two members of each independent sample pair with a fair coin. Conditional on the pooled data, the discrepancy for any fixed trace is an average of independent signed terms bounded in magnitude by 1. Hoeffding and a union bound over at most \(\Pi_{\mathcal H}(2n)\) pooled prediction traces give \[P\!\left(\sup_h|\widehat R(h)-R(h)|>\varepsilon\right) \le 4\Pi_{\mathcal H}(2n)e^{-n\varepsilon^2/8}\] under the usual measurability assumptions. This gives an order \(\sqrt{(d\log(en/d)+\log(1/\delta))/n}\) bound for the empirical-population gap. The quantitative fundamental theorem stated in the course gives agnostic sample complexity \(\Theta((d+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^2)\) and the textbook realizable bounds \(\Omega((d+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)\) and \(O((d\log(1/\varepsilon)+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)\) in their usual nontrivial parameter range. The sharper agnostic bound uses more than the one-scale union bound above. Together with the shattered-set lower bound, finite VC dimension characterizes distribution-free PAC learnability for binary classes under the standard regularity conditions. ChallengesProblem 1Find the VC dimension of all subsets of the real line that are unions of at most \(k\) intervals. Permit the empty set. Show solution The dimension is \(2k\). Among \(2k\) ordered points, any binary labeling has at most \(k\) contiguous runs of positives. Put one interval around each positive run, excluding neighboring negative points. For \(2k+1\) ordered points the alternating labeling starting and ending with 1 has \(k+1\) positive runs. Every interval joining any two of those runs contains a negative point. That labeling is impossible on every set of \(2k+1\) points. Problem 2Compare the VC dimensions of \(\mathbf1\{a\sin x>0\}\), \(\mathbf1\{\sin(x+a)>0\}\), and \(\mathbf1\{\sin(ax)>0\}\). Show solution The amplitude class has three distinct functions and can shatter one point, giving dimension 1. Phase shifts produce open semicircles of positives. The points \(0,\pi/2\) admit all four labels. Among three distinct points, either they cannot all fit in an open semicircle, or they can be ordered within one. In the latter case any open semicircle containing the two extremes contains the short arc between them, so the middle point cannot be negative. The dimension is 2. For frequency scaling use \(x_i=2^{i-1}\) for any \(n\). Given labels \(y_i\), put \(b_i=1-y_i\) and take \(a=2\pi(\sum_{j=1}^n b_j2^{-j}+2^{-n-1})\). The fractional part of \(ax_i/(2\pi)\) is \(b_i/2\) plus a number strictly between 0 and \(1/2\). Its sine is positive precisely when \(b_i=0\). Hence these \(n\) points are shattered for arbitrary \(n\). SourcesYang Yuan, Machine Learning (2026), Lecture 5 and Problem Sets 3–4. title: ACG 04: Projection and Learning on 3D Geometry
summary: Perspective projection maps three-dimensional positions to two-dimensional image coordinates. Single-view reconstruction asks what can be recovered after that mapping. Camera geometry identifies the missing con
body: Perspective projection maps three-dimensional positions to two-dimensional image coordinates. Single-view reconstruction asks what can be recovered after that mapping. Camera geometry identifies the missing constraints, and learning supplies priors about plausible scenes. Orthographic and perspective projectionUse a right-handed camera with forward axis \(-z\). Let \(n,f\) be the positive near and far distances, \(d=-z\), and set normalized depth to \([-1,1]\) with near mapping to \(-1\). Orthographic projection centers and scales each coordinate independently. For horizontal interval \([l,r]\), impose the two endpoint values to get \(x_{\mathrm{ndc}}=(2x-r-l)/(r-l)\). The same linear construction applies to vertical position and depth. Perspective instead projects along rays from the camera center. Let \(\phi\) be the vertical field of view and \(a\) the width-to-height ratio. The near plane’s half-height is \(n\tan(\phi/2)\), and similar triangles scale the near-plane intersection by \(n/d\). After normalization, \[x_{\mathrm{ndc}}=\frac{x}{ad\tan(\phi/2)},\qquad y_{\mathrm{ndc}}=\frac{y}{d\tan(\phi/2)}.\] Choose clip \(w_c=d\), making the homogeneous division produce the desired scale. Assume \(z_c=Az+B\) so normalized depth is \(-A+B/d\). Evaluating at \(d=n,f\) yields \(A=-(f+n)/(f-n)\) and \(B=-2fn/(f-n)\). For \(s=1/\tan(\phi/2)\), the projection matrix is \[P=\begin{pmatrix} s/a&0&0&0\\0&s&0&0\\ 0&0&-\frac{f+n}{f-n}&-\frac{2fn}{f-n}\\ 0&0&-1&0 \end{pmatrix}.\] The derivative of depth with respect to \(d\) is \(2fn/((f-n)d^2)\). Uniform quantization of projected depth therefore corresponds to coarser distance resolution farther away. A smaller near plane consumes more of the representable depth range near the eye. After clipping and division, a \(W\times H\) top-left-origin viewport maps NDC to \(x_s=W(x_{\mathrm{ndc}}+1)/2\) and \(y_s=H(1-y_{\mathrm{ndc}})/2\). Clip before the perspective divideThe visible clip-space region satisfies six linear half-space inequalities, such as \(w+x\ge0\) for the left boundary. An edge whose endpoints \(A,B\) lie on opposite sides of a clipping plane \(g(C)=0\) intersects it at \[t=\frac{g(A)}{g(A)-g(B)},\qquad C=(1-t)A+tB.\] Sutherland–Hodgman clipping processes one plane at a time. For each polygon edge, emit an intersection if membership changes and emit the next vertex if it is inside. Interpolate ordinary perspective-correct vertex attributes with the same \(t\) before dividing by \(w\). After all six planes, triangulate the clipped polygon and divide its retained vertices by \(w\). Performing clipping in screen space after division would mishandle edges that cross the eye plane. Choosing a representation for 3D learning Representation Useful computation Main tradeoff Multiview images Share a 2D encoder and aggregate features across views Occluded surfaces depend on viewpoint coverage Dense voxels Apply regular 3D kernels Doubling resolution per axis requires eight times as many cells Sparse voxels and octrees Process occupied cells or subdivide selected regions Neighbor lookup requires a spatial index or cross-level handling Point sets Process scan samples directly Sampling density varies and connectivity is absent Meshes Use face and edge structure and output a surface directly A deformable template generally retains its topology Implicit fields Query occupancy or distance at arbitrary coordinates Surface extraction requires additional queries Datasets differ in the signals available for training. ShapeNet studies object-level geometry, PartNet adds part hierarchies, ScanNet provides indoor observations, and HOI4D records interactions over time. An evaluation should state whether the input is a complete shape, a partial scan, or a changing scene. Set aggregation and local structurePointNet shares a feature extractor \(h\) across points, uses per-channel maxima, and applies an output head \(\gamma\): \[F(\{p_1,\ldots,p_m\})=\gamma\left(\max_i h(p_i)\right).\] Reordering the points reorders the feature rows, leaving each maximum unchanged. A perturbation that changes only points below all existing maxima can likewise leave the output unchanged. The same property limits the ability to infer density or local arrangements. PointNet++ selects local neighborhoods in the metric space, encodes relative coordinates in each neighborhood, and repeats the procedure at larger scales. PointNet · PointNet++ A simple implementation can use farthest-point sampling to choose neighborhood centers. Track the smallest squared distance from each point to any selected center, update the distance array after adding each center, and take its maximum for the next center. This costs \(O(mN)\) for \(m\) centers and \(N\) points, with \(O(N)\) memory. Gather neighbors for each center using a radius or nearest-neighbor query. Subtract the center coordinates so each local feature extractor sees the geometry of the patch. Single-view reconstruction objectivesScaling an object uniformly about the pinhole leaves its projected coordinates unchanged. Depth supervision can accommodate this ambiguity by comparing the shape of the predicted depth map up to one per-image scale. With \(\delta_i=\log\hat z_i-\log z_i\), minimize the squared error after adding a global offset \(\alpha\) to the predicted log depths. Differentiation gives \(\alpha=-\bar\delta\), and the minimized loss is \[\frac1m\sum_i\delta_i^2-\left(\frac1m\sum_i\delta_i\right)^2 .\] Point sets lack a canonical ordering, so a reconstruction can use the bidirectional squared Chamfer objective, \[D(P,Q)=\frac{1}{|P|}\sum_{p\in P}\min_{q\in Q}\|p-q\|^2 +\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{q\in Q}\min_{p\in P}\|q-p\|^2.\] The first term measures prediction accuracy and the second term measures coverage. Both are permutation invariant. Because a target can be reused as the closest neighbor of many different predictions, the objective gives limited control over sample density. Mesh prediction can instead deform a template, sample surface points for data terms, and regularize neighboring vertices and faces. A fixed template constrains changes to topology. Exercises Find precision loss. Under this projection, compare the world-space depth increments corresponding to an equal, infinitesimal NDC increment at \(d=2n\) and at \(d=20n\). Assume both are inside the frustum. Answer Invert \(dz_{\mathrm{ndc}}/dd=2fn/((f-n)d^2)\) locally. The distance increment scales as \(d^2\), so the farther sample’s increment is \(100\) times as large. Clip a segment. Against the left clip plane \(w+x=0\), clip the segment from \(A=(-3,0,0,1)\) to \(B=(0,2,0,2)\). Give the intersection and its screen \(y\) in NDC. Answer The signed values are \(g(A)=-2\) and \(g(B)=2\), giving \(t=1/2\). The intersection is \((-1.5,1,0,1.5)\), whose normalized \(y\) is \(2/3\). Interpolating the already-divided \(y\) values at the same parameter would give \(1/2\) and the wrong geometry. Separate ordinary and scale-invariant depth errors. The target depths are \((1,2,4)\) and predictions are \((2,4,4)\). Compute the optimal multiplicative correction and scale-invariant loss. Answer The log discrepancies are \((\log 2,\log 2,0)\) with mean \(2\log 2/3\). The scale correction is \(2^{-2/3}\), and the remaining variance is \(2(\log 2)^2/9\). ReferenceLi Yi, Advanced Computer Graphics, Lecture 4, “Learning + Geometry,” October 17, 2026, slides 3–32 for projection, 37–60 for datasets, 61–106 for analysis, and 107–144 for synthesis. title: ML 04: Matrix Completion and Nonconvex Geometry
summary: Derive the nuclear norm factorization, alternating least squares, and a strict-saddle example, then identify the information required for completion.
body:
Derive the nuclear norm factorization, alternating least squares, and a strict-saddle example, then identify the information required for completion. A rank-one fit recovers the hidden values in this connected synthetic observation pattern. The observation operatorA rating matrix \(M\in\mathbb R^{m	imes n}\) may have entries \(u_i^	op v_j\), where user and item vectors have dimension \(r\). This implies rank at most \(r\). The operator \(P_\Omega\) preserves observed entries and sets other entries to zero. Exact low-rank completion asks for \(\min_X\operatorname{rank}(X)\) subject to \(P_\Omega X=P_\Omega M\). Unobserved values are free variables. Fitting ordinary low-rank approximation to a zero-filled matrix includes artificial zero ratings in its objective. Low rank and identifiabilityFor an unobserved row of a rank-one matrix \(uv^	op\), the corresponding coordinate of \(u\) is undetermined. For \(M=e_ie_j^	op\), missing just entry \((i,j)\) leaves its scale undetermined. A recovery assumption should address both insufficient sampling and concentration of singular vectors. For a thin SVD \(M=U\Sigma V^	op\), typical incoherence conditions are \[\max_i\|U^	op e_i\|^2\le\mu r/m,\qquad \max_j\|V^	op e_j\|^2\le\mu r/n .\] The first quantities are diagonal entries of the orthogonal projector \(UU^	op\). They sum to \(\operatorname{tr}(UU^	op)=r\), so \(\mu\ge1\). A uniform unit singular vector attains \(\mu=1\), whereas a coordinate vector in \(\mathbb R^m\) needs \(\mu=m\). For a full-column-rank basis \(B\), calculate the same scores from \(\operatorname{diag}(B(B^	op B)^{-1}B^	op)\). Recovery results additionally depend on the sample size and selection process. From singular values to a convex objectiveThe nuclear norm \(\|X\|_\ast=\sum_i\sigma_i(X)\) is the dual of the spectral norm: writing \(X=\sum_i\sigma_i u_iv_i^	op\) gives \(\langle Z,Xangle\le\|Z\|_{m op}\sum_i\sigma_i\). Equality is achieved at \(Z=UV^	op\) with \(\|Z\|_{m op}=1\) for nonzero \(X\). As a supremum of linear functions it is convex. Moreover, for factor widths at least \(\operatorname{rank}(X)\), \[\|X\|_\ast=\min_{AB^	op=X}	frac12(\|A\|_F^2+\|B\|_F^2).\] To attain the bound take \(A=U\Sigma^{1/2}\) and \(B=V\Sigma^{1/2}\). For the other direction, any \(\|Z\|_{m op}\le1\) satisfies \(\langle Z,AB^	opangle=\langle Z^	op A,Bangle\le\|A\|_F\|B\|_F\le(\|A\|_F^2+\|B\|_F^2)/2\). Maximize over \(Z\). The identity connects convex nuclear-norm penalization to Frobenius-regularized factor fitting, where fixing a narrower factor width imposes an additional rank constraint. Alternating minimization and strict saddlesFor \[F(A,B)=	frac12\sum_{(i,j)\in\Omega}(a_i^	op b_j-M_{ij})^2 +	frac\lambda2(\|A\|_F^2+\|B\|_F^2),\] holding \(B\) fixed gives independent row subproblems, with normal equation \[\left(\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\Omega}b_jb_j^	op+\lambda Iight)a_i =\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\Omega}M_{ij}b_j.\] The update for \(B\) interchanges the roles. Exact subproblem solutions never increase \(F\). For the product alone, \((A,B)\mapsto(AR,BR^{-	op})\) preserves every prediction for invertible \(R\). The Frobenius regularizer preserves this symmetry for orthogonal \(R\). For \(F(a,b)=	frac12(ab-1)^2\), the gradient vanishes at \((0,0)\). The Hessian there is \[ egin{pmatrix}0&-1\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\] with eigenvalues \(\pm1\). Taylor expansion along \((1,1)\) gives local decrease and expansion along \((1,-1)\) gives local increase. The functions \(t^4,-t^4,t^3\) all have first and second derivatives zero at the origin, yet give a local minimum, a local maximum, and neither. Negative curvature supplies information that flat second-order stationarity lacks. The three regions in a strict-saddle analysisWith an unbiased perturbation \(\xi\) of conditional second moment at most \(\sigma^2\), the \(L\)-smooth update \(w^+=w-\eta(
abla f(w)+\xi)\) gives \[\mathbb E[f(w^+)-f(w)\mid w]\le -\eta(1-L\eta/2)\|
abla f(w)\|^2+	frac{L\eta^2}{2}\sigma^2.\] This follows by expanding the upper quadratic bound and dropping the cross term in expectation. A sufficiently large gradient produces a quantitative decrease. In the negative-curvature region, suppose \(H=
abla^2 f(w)\) has a unit eigenvector \(v\) of eigenvalue \(-\gamma<0\). In the quadratic model about \(w\), iteration has linear part \(I-\eta H\) and amplifies a displacement along \(v\) by \(1+\eta\gamma\). A perturbation with enough mass along \(v\) can seed this displacement. For an \(M\)-Lipschitz Hessian, subtracting the linear gradient expansion leaves a remainder bounded by \(M\|z\|^2/2\) at displacement \(z\), by integrating the Hessian difference along the segment. This controls the approximation over a small neighborhood. In particular, a direct signed step of radius \(r\) along \(v\), choosing the sign for a nonpositive linear term, gives \(f(w\pm rv)-f(w)\le-\gamma r^2/2+Mr^3/6\). Near a local minimum, favorable curvature and sufficiently small steps and perturbations help keep iterates inside its basin. If the conditional probability of exiting in a step is bounded by \(p\) while still inside, the chance of any exit within \(T\) steps is at most \(Tp\) by a union bound on the first exit. The course’s informal strict-saddle guarantee combines these three regions: outside the basin there must be quantitative decrease over one or more steps, and a lower bound on the objective limits the number of such stages. Recovery additionally depends on identifiability. A global minimizer of the observed objective can still fail to recover \(M\). ChallengesProblem 1Suppose every observed value of a nonzero rank-one matrix is nonzero. Give necessary and sufficient graph conditions for unique rank-one completion among real matrices, including vertices with no observed edges. Show solution View rows and columns as vertices of a bipartite graph with observed entries as edges. If the graph is connected, fix one nonzero factor coordinate as a gauge and propagate each adjacent factor by dividing the edge value by the known coordinate. Existence of the given completion ensures consistency around cycles. All factors are then determined up to one global rescaling and every product is fixed. If an isolated row or column is present, its factor can vary while preserving the observations and changing at least one unobserved product. If two components contain edges, independently rescale the row factors in one by \(c\) and the column factors there by \(1/c\). Cross-component entries change. In the no-observation case a real rank-one completion is plainly nonunique. Problem 2A \(4	imes4\) matrix has its first two rows equal to \((9,0,1,0)\) and the other two equal to \((2,2,2,2)\). Compute its smallest joint incoherence constant without an SVD. Show solution The column projector has constant diagonal \(1/2\). For the row projector, form \(B\) from the distinct rows and use \(B^	op(BB^	op)^{-1}B\). The inner inverse is \( rac1{912} igl( egin{smallmatrix}16&-20\-20&82\end{smallmatrix} igr)\). The four column quadratic forms give the diagonal \((113,41,33,41)/114\). The rank is 2, so the joint constant is \((4/2)\max\{1/2,113/114\}=113/57\). SourcesYang Yuan, Machine Learning (2026), Lecture 4 and Problem Set 3. The chapter’s course supplements discuss matrix completion, incoherence, and escaping saddle points. title: ACG 03: Transformations, Rotations, and Camera Frames
summary: A transformation can move a point in one coordinate system or express the same point in another. In either case, name the source and destination frames and check the origin and basis vectors before composing ma
body: A transformation can move a point in one coordinate system or express the same point in another. In either case, name the source and destination frames and check the origin and basis vectors before composing matrices. Affine transformations and homogeneous coordinatesWith column vectors, the affine map \(x'=Ax+t\) becomes \[\begin{pmatrix}x'\\1\end{pmatrix}= \begin{pmatrix}A&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}x\\1\end{pmatrix}.\] The difference of two point vectors has homogeneous component zero, so translations leave displacement vectors unchanged. A rotation around \(c\) is \(T(c)RT(-c)\), applied from right to left. The expression \(R(x-c)+c\) immediately verifies that the pivot remains fixed. For invertible \(A\), the inverse map is \(A^{-1}x'-A^{-1}t\). Normal vectors follow a different rule. If \(n^\mathsf T u=0\) for a tangent \(u\), require \(n'^\mathsf T Au=0\). Choosing \(n'=A^{-\mathsf T}n\) preserves the dot product. Normalize afterward when a shader expects unit length. Using \(An\) works for rotations and uniform scaling up to normalization, but nonuniform scaling can break orthogonality. PBRT, “Transformations” Rotations and the exponential mapA rotation preserves inner products, so \(R^\mathsf T R=I\). Its determinant is \(1\) because it also preserves orientation. These matrices form \(SO(3)\). Their inverses are transposes, and their products remain rotations. Let \(u\) be a unit axis and set \(Kv=u\times v\). The triple product gives \(K^2=uu^\mathsf T-I\) and \(K^3=-K\). Summing the odd and even terms of the exponential power series yields Rodrigues’ formula, \[R=e^{\theta K}=I+\sin\theta\,K+(1-\cos\theta)K^2.\] In an orthonormal basis with \(u\) as one axis, \(R\) consists of a planar rotation block and an unchanged axis. Taking the trace gives \(\operatorname{tr}R=1+2\cos\theta\). Apply this identity to \(R_1^\mathsf T R_2\) to recover the angle between two orientations. The identity rotation has no unique axis. At angle \(\pi\), an axis and its negative define the same rotation. Euler angles and quaternionsEuler angles depend on the rotation convention. For \(R=R_z(\gamma)R_y(\beta)R_x(\alpha)\), at \(\beta=\pi/2\) the \(x\) axis rotates onto \(-z\). Conjugating the rotation around \(x\) then gives \[R_z(\gamma)R_y(\pi/2)R_x(\alpha)=R_z(\gamma-\alpha)R_y(\pi/2).\] The two angles \(\gamma,\alpha\) no longer have independent effects. This is gimbal lock. The unit quaternion \(q=(\cos(\theta/2),u\sin(\theta/2))\) rotates a vector through \((0,v')=q(0,v)q^{-1}\). Expanding the vector part gives \[\cos\theta\,v+(1-\cos\theta)u(u^\mathsf Tv)+\sin\theta\,(u\times v),\] the same Rodrigues formula. Since the signs cancel in the sandwich product, \(q\) and \(-q\) encode one rotation. Implement shortest-arc spherical interpolationTwo unit quaternions span a two-dimensional plane in four dimensions. In that plane, the geodesic interpolation at fraction \(t\) combines them with sine weights. Flipping the endpoint representative when the dot product is negative chooses the shorter rotation path. The normalized linear limit avoids division by a tiny sine when the inputs are nearly equal. 12345678910111213from math import acos, sindef slerp(q0, q1, t): d = dot(q0, q1) if d < 0: q1, d = -q1, -d d = min(1.0, d) if d > 0.9995: return normalize((1 - t)*q0 + t*q1) omega = acos(d) a = sin((1 - t)*omega) / sin(omega) b = sin(t*omega) / sin(omega) return a*q0 + b*q1 The function assumes unit inputs, and the result represents \(q_0\) at \(t=0\) and the orientation of \(q_1\) at \(t=1\). When \(q_1=-q_0\), the entire interpolation represents the same orientation. The view matrixLet \(e\) be the camera center and let \(r,u,b\) denote its right, up, and backward unit vectors. Put the basis vectors into the columns of \(R\). The camera looks along its local negative \(z\) axis. Its camera-to-world map is \(p_w=Rp_c+e\), so \[p_c=R^\mathsf T(p_w-e),\qquad V=\begin{pmatrix}R^\mathsf T&-R^\mathsf T e\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\] For target \(a\) and reference up vector \(u_0\), use \(b=\operatorname{normalize}(e-a)\), \(r=\operatorname{normalize}(u_0\times b)\), and \(u=b\times r\). A reference up parallel to \(b\) fails to determine the roll. The implementation should check that the camera center maps to the origin and that \(e-\lambda b\) with \(\lambda>0\) maps to negative local \(z\). The model-view composition is \(VM\), followed by the projection in Lecture 4. Exercises Construct the correct normal. The plane \(x+y=0\) undergoes scaling by \(\operatorname{diag}(2,1,3)\). Derive its transformed equation and normal. Explain why applying the same matrix to the original normal disagrees. Answer Solve for the old coordinates to obtain \(x'/2+y'=0\). The new normal is proportional to \((1/2,1,0)\), given by the inverse transpose. Multiplying directly gives \((2,1,0)\), whose dot product with the transformed tangent \((2,-1,0)\) is \(3\). Move the model and camera together. Let a rigid motion \(T\) transform both the camera-to-world matrix \(C\) and the model-to-world matrix \(M\). Prove that camera-space geometry is invariant. Answer After the motion, the product is \((TC)^{-1}(TM)=C^{-1}T^{-1}TM=C^{-1}M\). The camera senses relative placement, so the common world-space motion cancels. Quaternion sign and timing. Interpolate from identity to a \(270^\circ\) rotation about \(z\) via shortest-arc SLERP. What orientation is represented at \(t=1/2\)? Answer The endpoint quaternion has negative real part \(\cos 135^\circ\). Its negation represents a \(-90^\circ\) turn about \(z\). The shortest arc begins at identity and ends at this signed angle, so its midpoint represents \(-45^\circ\) about \(z\). ReferenceLi Yi, Advanced Computer Graphics, Lecture 3, “Transformation,” September 30, 2026, slides 50–81 for affine maps, 82–125 for rotations, and 126–137 for camera frames. title: ML 03: SGD, SVRG, and Mirror Descent
summary: Prove a convergence bound for averaged SGD, derive SVRG’s epoch contraction, and extend descent to the geometry of a probability simplex.
body:
Prove a convergence bound for averaged SGD, derive SVRG’s epoch contraction, and extend descent to the geometry of a probability simplex. The horizontal axis counts component-gradient evaluations, including the full gradient at each SVRG snapshot. The illustrated snapshots use the last inner iterate. Which iterate does SGD control?Let \(f\) be convex and \(L\)-smooth with minimizer \(w^\star\), and set \(w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta G_t\). Conditional on the history \(\mathcal F_t\) before sampling the next direction, assume \(\mathbb E_tG_t=g_t=

title: ACG 02: Curves, Meshes, and Implicit Surfaces
summary: A parametric surface answers “where is the point at these coordinates?” An implicit field answers “what is the value at this position?” A triangle mesh answers questions about connectivity. These different quer
body: A parametric surface answers “where is the point at these coordinates?” An implicit field answers “what is the value at this position?” A triangle mesh answers questions about connectivity. These different query types explain why a graphics system often uses several geometry representations for the same object. Constructing a Bézier curveGiven control points \(P_0,\ldots,P_n\), repeatedly interpolate adjacent points. Set \(P_i^{(0)}=P_i\) and \[P_i^{(k)}(t)=(1-t)P_i^{(k-1)}(t)+tP_{i+1}^{(k-1)}(t).\] Expanding the recursion reveals how many ways each control point reaches the output. A path from \(P_i\) takes \(i\) right branches and \(n-i\) left branches, so the coefficient is \(\binom ni t^i(1-t)^{n-i}\). This gives the Bernstein form \[B(t)=\sum_{i=0}^n P_i b_{i,n}(t),\qquad b_{i,n}(t)=\binom ni t^i(1-t)^{n-i}.\] On \([0,1]\), the weights are nonnegative and sum to \((t+1-t)^n=1\). Hence the curve lies in the convex hull of the control polygon, and affine maps commute with evaluation. Differentiating a basis polynomial yields \(b'_{i,n}=n(b_{i-1,n-1}-b_{i,n-1})\), with out-of-range terms set to zero. Reindexing the derivative gives \[B'(t)=n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(P_{i+1}-P_i)b_{i,n-1}(t).\] For two consecutive cubics \(P\) and \(Q\), position continuity requires \(P_3=Q_0\). If their durations are \(h_P,h_Q\), matching derivatives in global time requires \((P_3-P_2)/h_P=(Q_1-Q_0)/h_Q\). Merely matching the direction of their nonzero tangent vectors gives geometric \(G^1\) continuity. Hermite curves encode tangents directly, while B-splines use basis functions with local support to control long curves. Subdivision with de CasteljauEach level of interpolation produces the endpoints of a smaller control polygon on both sides of the split. The following algorithm returns the control polygons for the intervals \([0,t]\) and \([t,1]\), each reparametrized locally to \([0,1]\). 123456789def split_bezier(points, t): row = list(points) left = [row[0]] right = [row[-1]] while len(row) > 1: row = [(1 - t)*a + t*b for a, b in zip(row, row[1:])] left.append(row[0]) right.append(row[-1]) return left, list(reversed(right)) The two outputs share their endpoint \(B(t)\). The algorithm takes quadratic time in the degree and linear auxiliary space. To tessellate for display, split in object space, project each child control polygon, and compare its control points with the chord between its endpoints. For a child whose clip-space weights are all positive, the projected curve is a rational Bézier curve with nonnegative normalized weights. It stays in the convex hull of the projected control points, so their greatest distance to the chord segment bounds the curve’s distance as well. Under perspective projection, splitting the ordinary 2D polygon alone would compute a different curve. For tensor-product surfaces, evaluate one set of control curves along \(u\) and then evaluate the resulting control polygon along \(v\): \[S(u,v)=\sum_{i,j}P_{ij}b_{i,m}(u)b_{j,n}(v).\] At a regular point, the cross product \(S_u\times S_v\) is perpendicular to both tangent directions and gives a normal after normalization. Point clouds and meshesA point cloud stores samples, optionally with normals or appearance attributes. To sample an indexed mesh uniformly over area, select a face with probability equal to its fraction of total area. Draw uniform \(u,v\in[0,1]\). If \(u+v>1\), replace them by \(1-u,1-v\). The two halves of the square now map onto the same parameter triangle by an area-preserving transformation. The affine map \(A+u(B-A)+v(C-A)\) preserves uniformity inside the selected face. A triangle uses its index order to determine normal direction via \((B-A)\times(C-A)\). In a two-manifold triangle mesh, each interior edge belongs to two faces and each boundary edge to one. Each vertex link must also form a single cycle or path. Two triangles touching only at a vertex obey the edge-count test but give that shared vertex a disconnected neighborhood. Subdivision, simplification, and deformationLoop subdivision replaces each triangle with four smaller triangles and updates vertex positions. For interior edge \(AB\) and opposite vertices \(C,D\), the new edge point is \(\tfrac38(A+B)+\tfrac18(C+D)\). Catmull–Clark uses input faces, edges, and vertices to create new quadrilateral faces. Creases and boundaries require their own stencils. Quadric error metrics simplify meshes by prioritizing inexpensive edge collapses. The squared distance to a plane \(n^\mathsf T x+d=0\) with unit \(n\) is \((p^\mathsf T\tilde x)^2\) for \(p=(n,d)\) and \(\tilde x=(x,1)\). Accumulating these penalties gives \(Q=\sum pp^\mathsf T\). Merge the two endpoint quadrics when collapsing an edge. Partitioning \(Q\) yields \[E(x)=x^\mathsf T A x+2b^\mathsf T x+c,\qquad \nabla E(x)=2Ax+2b.\] The optimum is \(-A^{-1}b\) when \(A\) is invertible. In a locally flat region, the error may leave the two tangent directions unconstrained. Evaluate the original endpoints or optimize along their segment. Reject collapses that invalidate connectivity or flip protected faces. As-rigid-as-possible deformation minimizes discrepancies between new edges and locally rotated original edges, \[E=\sum_i\sum_{j\in N(i)}w_{ij}\|(p'_i-p'_j)-R_i(p_i-p_j)\|^2,\qquad R_i\in SO(3).\] A common rigid transform \(p_i'=Rp_i+t\) gives zero error. The translation cancels in edge differences and every \(R_i\) can equal \(R\). Fix some handle positions, alternate estimating the rotations and solving the linear system for positions, and stop when the energy changes little. Free-form deformation shapes space itself by interpolating displacements on a control lattice. Implicit geometryA sphere signed distance field is \(F(x)=\|x-c\|-r\). For a differentiable regular level set, differentiating \(F(x(s))=0\) along a surface curve gives \(\nabla F\cdot x'(s)=0\). Thus the gradient supplies a normal candidate. With negative values inside, a point lies in the union if \(\min(F_A,F_B)<0\), in the intersection if \(\max(F_A,F_B)<0\), and in the interior of the difference if \(F_A<0<F_B\). A combined field preserves these sign tests while its values can lose the exact distance interpretation. Sample the field on a grid and extract a triangulated isosurface when an explicit surface is needed. Exercises Unequal segment durations. A cubic ends at \(P_3=(2,1)\) and approaches it from \(P_2=(1,0)\). It takes three seconds. The next cubic takes one second. Find its first two control points for \(C^1\) continuity. Answer Take \(Q_0=P_3=(2,1)\). Matching \(3(P_3-P_2)/3\) to \(3(Q_1-Q_0)/1\) gives \(Q_1=(7/3,4/3)\). Choosing \(Q_1=(3,2)\) matches direction but triples the global speed at the join. Singular QEM. The contributing planes are \(x=0\) and \(y=0\). Find all minimizers and then find the optimal point on the segment from \((1,0,1)\) to \((0,1,3)\). Answer The energy is \(x^2+y^2\), so every point on the \(z\) axis is an unconstrained minimizer. Along the segment, \(E(s)=(1-s)^2+s^2\) is minimized at \(s=1/2\), giving \((1/2,1/2,2)\) with energy \(1/2\). CSG distance. Let \(F_A(x)=|x|-2\) and \(F_B(x)=|x-1|-2\) on the real line. Show why the minimum field preserves the union’s sign while failing to give exact signed distance at \(x=0.5\). Answer The solid intervals are \([-2,2]\) and \([-1,3]\), giving union \([-2,3]\). At \(x=0.5\), both fields are \(-1.5\), but the nearest union boundary is \(2.5\) units away. The exact signed distance is \(-2.5\). ReferenceLi Yi, Advanced Computer Graphics, Lecture 2, “Geometry,” September 23, 2026, slides 15–55 for curves and surfaces, 57–96 for representations, and 97–152 for mesh processing and implicit geometry. title: ML 02: Gradient Descent and Convergence
summary: Derive gradient descent from the smoothness bound and prove its rates for convex, strongly convex, and nonconvex objectives.
body:
Derive gradient descent from the smoothness bound and prove its rates for convex, strongly convex, and nonconvex objectives. The larger stable step oscillates along the high-curvature axis. The small step follows a smoother path. Smoothness gives a quadratic boundOn an unconstrained Euclidean space the step is \(x^+=x-\eta
abla f(x)\). It minimizes the quadratic local model \(\langle
abla f(x),dangle+\|d\|^2/(2\eta)\) over the displacement \(d\). For an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, integrate along \(d=y-x\): \[ egin{aligned} f(y)-f(x)-\langle

Integrating the Hessian along the segment then gives the original Lipschitz condition. Analogously the lower remainder bound \(\mu\|d\|^2/2\) is equivalent to \(
abla^2f\succeq\mu I\). In one direction, take the directional limit. In the other, apply convexity to \(f(x)-\mu\|x\|^2/2\) using its positive semidefinite Hessian. Convexity itself is the \(\mu=0\) case. Two other forms follow from the same argument. Apply Jensen’s inequality to \(f-\mu\|\cdot\|^2/2\) and expand the square: \[f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)-	frac\mu2 t(1-t)\|x-y\|^2.\] Conversely, subtracting the quadratic converts this inequality into ordinary convexity. For differentiable \(f\), add the lower remainder bounds with \(x,y\) exchanged to obtain strong gradient monotonicity, \[\langle
abla f(y)-
abla f(x),y-xangle\ge\mu\|y-x\|^2.\] Conversely, apply that inequality to \(x\) and \(x+td\). For \(t>0\) divide by \(t\) to give \(\langle
abla f(x+td)-
abla f(x),dangle\ge\mu t\|d\|^2\). Integrating from zero to one gives the lower remainder bound. With \(d=-\eta g\), \(g=
abla f(x)\), smoothness yields \[f(x^+)\le f(x)-\eta(1-L\eta/2)\|g\|^2.\] For \(0<\eta\le1/L\), the decrease is at least \(\eta\|g\|^2/2\). Convex objectivesConvexity gives \(f(x)-f^\star\le\langle g,x-x^\starangle\) for any minimizer \(x^\star\). Combine this with the decrease and expand the next squared distance: \[f(x_{t+1})-f^\star\le \langle g_t,x_t-x^\starangle-	frac\eta2\|g_t\|^2 = rac{\|x_t-x^\star\|^2-\|x_{t+1}-x^\star\|^2}{2\eta}.\] Sum from \(t=0\) to \(T-1\). The distances telescope. Since the losses are nonincreasing, the last loss is at most their average, giving \(f(x_T)-f^\star\le\|x_0-x^\star\|^2/(2\eta T)\). Strong convexityThe \(\mu\)-strongly convex lower quadratic model has minimum \(f(x)-\|
abla f(x)\|^2/(2\mu)\). Evaluating the lower bound at a minimizer shows \(f(x)-f^\star\le\|
abla f(x)\|^2/(2\mu)\). Plugging this into descent with \(\eta=1/L\) yields \[f(x_T)-f^\star\le (1-\mu/L)^T[f(x_0)-f^\star].\] For a quadratic with Hessian \(A\), the \(i\)th eigencoordinate is multiplied by \(1-\eta\lambda_i\) each step. A large ratio \(L/\mu\) means a step chosen for the steep direction can move slowly along the shallow direction. Nonconvex objectivesIf \(f\) is smooth and bounded below, summing the decrease yields \[\min_{0\le t<T}\|
abla f(x_t)\|^2\le  rac{2(f(x_0)-\inf f)}{\eta T}.\] This controls a first-order stationary point. For example, \(x^2-y^2+y^4\) is bounded below and has a stationary point at the origin, where the Hessian has one negative eigenvalue. A twice differentiable local minimizer has zero gradient and a positive semidefinite Hessian by restriction to lines. If its Hessian is positive definite, Taylor’s theorem gives a strict local minimum. Full gradients for \(f=n^{-1}\sum_i f_i\) cost \(n\) component gradients. Uniform subsampling gives a cheaper unbiased direction whose variance and convergence properties are addressed in Lecture 3. title: ACG 01: Introduction to Computer Graphics
summary: A rendered image is the result of a computation. Geometry specifies what is in the scene. Materials and light determine surface appearance, the camera selects a viewpoint, and the display reproduces the resulti
body: A rendered image is the result of a computation. Geometry specifies what is in the scene. Materials and light determine surface appearance, the camera selects a viewpoint, and the display reproduces the resulting samples. Separating these inputs makes it possible to explain a visual effect and test its cause. From a 3D scene to a 2D imageWrite a scene as \(\mathcal S=(G,M,L,C)\), with geometry, materials, lights, and a camera. Rendering computes \(I=\mathcal R(\mathcal S)\). Changing only \(C\) isolates the effects of perspective and visibility. Changing only \(M\) or \(L\) exposes how reflectance and illumination interact. Computer vision often reverses part of this computation by estimating scene properties from images. For a pinhole camera looking along positive \(Z\), put the virtual image plane at \(Z=f\). The ray through a point \(P=(X,Y,Z)\) meets the image plane at \((fX/Z,fY/Z,f)\). Both coordinates follow from scaling the vector \(P\) by \(f/Z\). \[(x,y)=\left(f\frac{X}{Z},f\frac{Y}{Z}\right).\] Multiplying all coordinates by any positive \(\lambda\) leaves the image point unchanged. One view constrains a point to a ray. Given a second calibrated camera and a corresponding image point, intersecting two rays adds a depth constraint. Closely spaced cameras yield nearly parallel rays for distant objects, so small observation errors can still produce large depth errors. Modeling, motion, and displayA triangle mesh stores positions and the connections between them. It can attach surface normals, texture coordinates, and materials to its vertices or faces. An implicit model defines a surface through a zero set, such as \(F(x)=\|x-c\|^2-r^2=0\) for a sphere. This sphere function makes containment a sign test. A mesh makes it straightforward to enumerate and transform the triangles of a surface. The rendering and modeling operations determine which representation is useful. Animation adds time. When an animator specifies two positions at times \(t_0,t_1\), linear interpolation gives \[p(t)=(1-s)p_0+sp_1,\qquad s=\frac{t-t_0}{t_1-t_0}.\] The derivative is \((p_1-p_0)/(t_1-t_0)\) throughout the interval. Matching the endpoints of consecutive segments creates continuous positions while still allowing an abrupt velocity change. Skeletal animation propagates joint transformations down a hierarchy and uses them to move skin vertices. Physical simulation advances positions and velocities using forces and constraints. A spring with rest length \(\ell_0\) stores \(\tfrac12 k(\ell-\ell_0)^2\) of potential energy and exerts the restoring force \(-k(\ell-\ell_0)\) along its extension coordinate. A framebuffer holds discrete image samples before display encoding. Let \(g\) map a linear intensity to a display code. Equal-area averaging belongs in linear space, so the encoded average of intensities \(a,b\) is \(g((a+b)/2)\). For a nonlinear \(g\), this generally differs from \((g(a)+g(b))/2\). The same distinction matters in texture filtering and alpha compositing. Two rendering algorithmsRasterization projects primitives and enumerates the samples they cover. At an opaque pixel, a depth test keeps the nearest submitted fragment. Triangle projection, coverage, and shading can therefore be divided into pipeline stages. Ray casting starts at the camera and queries the scene for the first hit along each sample ray. A second ray toward a point light tests whether the surface receives direct light. Recursive or sampled rays can estimate mirror reflections, refractions, and indirect light. Both rasterization and ray tracing compute visibility, but their loop orders differ: rasterization starts with primitives, while ray casting starts with samples. Implement a minimal pinhole rendererUse a horizontal and vertical pixel scale \(f_x,f_y\) and zero-based coordinates referenced to the image’s upper-left corner. The image center is \((c_x,c_y)\). The following sketch assumes an orthonormal camera basis and ray depth increasing forward. 123456789101112def camera_ray(i, j, camera): x = (i + 0.5 - camera.cx) / camera.fx y = (camera.cy - j - 0.5) / camera.fy direction = normalize(camera.right*x + camera.up*y + camera.forward) return Ray(camera.center, direction)def render_pixel(i, j, camera, scene): ray = camera_ray(i, j, camera) hit = scene.closest_hit(ray, t_min=0) if hit is None: return scene.background(ray.direction) return 0.5 * (hit.normal + Vec3(1, 1, 1)) This version visualizes normal orientation, making it easy to check geometry and camera conventions before adding shading. A plane with unit normal \((0,1,0)\) should give the same color \((0.5,1,0.5)\) wherever it appears. An object translated directly along the optical axis stays centered but changes size. For a surface patch parallel to the image plane and doubled in depth, its apparent linear extent halves. Exercises Stereo conditioning. Two identical rectified cameras share one image plane orientation. The right camera is displaced by \(b\) along \(X\). Derive depth from the measured disparity and quantify the first-order error when the disparity changes by \(\delta d\). Answer With the same focal length \(f\), the projected coordinates are \(x_L=fX/Z\) and \(x_R=f(X-b)/Z\). Thus \(d=x_L-x_R=fb/Z\), so \(Z=fb/d\) and \(\delta Z\approx-fb\,\delta d/d^2\). At fixed baseline and focal length, the absolute depth error grows quadratically with distance for constant disparity error. Repair a velocity discontinuity. An object must go from \(0\) to \(1\) in one second, with zero velocity at each endpoint. Find the cubic of lowest possible degree that satisfies the constraints, and calculate its peak velocity. Answer The conditions at zero give \(p(t)=at^3+bt^2\). At one, \(a+b=1\) and \(3a+2b=0\), so \(p(t)=3t^2-2t^3\). Its derivative \(6t(1-t)\) reaches \(1.5\) at \(t=1/2\). A quadratic with derivative zero at two distinct points would have a derivative identically zero, so the cubic is minimal. Diagnose incorrect compositing. With display encoding \(g(L)=\sqrt L\), a pixel straddles equal areas of white and black. Compare the displayed linear intensity from averaging codes with the physically correct result. Answer Averaging codes gives \((g(0)+g(1))/2=0.5\). The display decodes that to \(L=0.25\). Equal illuminated areas average to \(L=0.5\), which should be encoded as \(1/\sqrt 2\). Code-space averaging makes this edge too dark. ReferenceLi Yi, Advanced Computer Graphics, Lecture 1, “Introduction,” September 16, 2026. The pinhole derivation and diagnostic renderer develop the lecture’s image-formation examples. Course notes · Next lecture

title: ML 01: Supervised Learning, Risk, and Data
summary: Derive the optimal predictions under squared and classification loss, then trace how training data, validation, and deployment define different risks.
body: Derive the optimal predictions under squared and classification loss, then trace how training data, validation, and deployment define different risks. The training samples contain noise. The test curve compares predictions on a dense grid with the noiseless function. Empirical and population riskGiven independent draws \(S=\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\) from a distribution \(P\), a loss \(\ell\), and a hypothesis class \(\mathcal H\), empirical risk minimization solves \[\widehat h\in\arg\min_{h\in\mathcal H}\widehat R_S(h), \qquad \widehat R_S(h)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(h(x_i),y_i).\] The population risk is \(R(h)=\mathbb E_P[\ell(h(X),Y)]\). For a fixed predictor independent of \(S\), \(\mathbb E_S[\widehat R_S(h)]=R(h)\) by linearity. The model \(\widehat h(S)\) depends on the sample. For every fixed \(h\), \(\mathbb E\widehat R_S(\widehat h)\le\mathbb E\widehat R_S(h)=R(h)\), while \(\mathbb E R(\widehat h)\ge\inf_{h\in\mathcal H}R(h)\). Fitting and evaluating on the same data can therefore produce an optimistic estimate. For example, a flexible model can memorize independent fair-coin labels on distinct training inputs, while any prediction for an independent input is correct with probability \(1/2\). Optimal prediction depends on the lossWrite \(m(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]\). Expanding the squared error about \(m(x)\) kills its cross term after conditioning: \[\mathbb E[(Y-a)^2\mid X=x]=\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X=x)+(m(x)-a)^2.\] The conditional mean minimizes squared loss. For absolute loss, the left and right derivatives of the conditional objective are \(2P(Y<a\mid x)-1\) and \(2P(Y\le a\mid x)-1\). Their interval contains zero precisely at a conditional median. For binary classification let \(\eta(x)=P(Y=1\mid X=x)\). Predicting 0 incurs conditional error \(\eta(x)\) and predicting 1 incurs \(1-\eta(x)\), so \[h^\star(x)=\mathbf1\{\eta(x)\ge\tfrac12\},\qquad R(h^\star)=\mathbb E\min\{\eta(X),1-\eta(X)\}.\] With false-positive cost \(c_{\rm FP}\) and false-negative cost \(c_{\rm FN}\), compare \(c_{\rm FP}(1-\eta)\) and \(c_{\rm FN}\eta\). The optimal positive threshold is \(c_{\rm FP}/(c_{\rm FP}+c_{\rm FN})\). Choosing a model and estimating its performanceThe training set determines parameters. A validation set chooses polynomial degree, regularization strength, or training duration. Once these choices are fixed, an independent test set estimates performance. In \(k\)-fold cross-validation, fit on \(k-1\) folds and predict on the omitted fold, repeating until every example has a held-out prediction. Fit standardization and feature selection inside each training fold. Group related measurements by entity and split forecasting data by time. Otherwise the evaluation can reuse information that would be unavailable at prediction time. Increasing polynomial degree enlarges the hypothesis class, so training error cannot increase: the previous solution remains feasible. Test error can rise as the model becomes more sensitive to sample noise. An explicit tradeoff is \(\min_w\widehat R_S(h_w)+\lambda\|w\|_2^2\). The optimizer and the statistical guarantees for such objectives are developed in Lecture 2 and Lecture 5. Dataset construction and unlabeled dataLabeling pipelines can separate candidate selection, annotation, and verification. For object masks, a disagreement between annotators can reflect ambiguity in the target definition. The sampling plan should reflect the deployment distribution, including entities and acquisition conditions. Clustering, PCA, and generative modeling infer structure from \(X\). Semi-supervised methods add information when a relationship between \(P_X\) and \(P(Y\mid X)\) is assumed. For example, a decision boundary might pass through regions of low input density. Holding \(P_X\) fixed leaves many possible label rules, all consistent with the same unlabeled observations. A Chernoff calculation for demandIf \(X_i\) are independent Bernoulli variables and \(Z=\sum_i X_i\) has mean \(\mu\), then for \(t>0\), \[\mathbb E e^{tZ}=\prod_i (1+p_i(e^t-1))\le \exp(\mu(e^t-1)).\] By Markov’s inequality, \(P(Z\ge(1+a)\mu)\le e^{\mu(e^t-1)-t(1+a)\mu}\). The minimizing \(t=\log(1+a)\) gives \(\exp(-\mu[(1+a)\log(1+a)-a])\). This controls the probability that independent requests exceed a capacity set above the mean. ChallengesProblem 1Show that the excess 0–1 risk of a plug-in classifier \(\widehat h=\mathbf1\{\widehat\eta\ge1/2\}\) is at most \(2\mathbb E|\widehat\eta(X)-\eta(X)|\). If \(\|\widehat\eta-\eta\|_\infty\le a\) and \(P(|\eta(X)-1/2|\le t)\le Ct^\kappa\), strengthen the rate. Show solution At a point of disagreement with the Bayes rule, the additional conditional error is \(|2\eta(x)-1|\). Disagreement implies \(|\eta(x)-1/2|\le|\widehat\eta(x)-\eta(x)|\), because the two scores straddle the threshold. Take expectations. Under the uniform bound, all disagreements lie in the band of width \(a\) and their conditional cost is at most \(2a\), so the excess risk is at most \(2Ca^{\kappa+1}\). Problem 2Given \(M\) candidate predictors trained independently of a validation set of \(n\) examples with losses in \([0,1]\), give a high-probability bound on the selected candidate’s excess risk. What role does independence play? Show solution Conditioned on the candidates, Hoeffding and a union bound put all empirical risks within \(\varepsilon/2\) of their true risks except with probability \(2M e^{-n\varepsilon^2/2}\). The selected function then has excess risk at most \(\varepsilon\) by two applications of the deviation bound and empirical optimality. Thus \(n\ge 2\log(2M/\delta)/\varepsilon^2\) suffices. Adaptive candidate construction changes the law of the validation sample conditional on those functions, so the fixed-candidate concentration need not apply. SourcesYang Yuan, Machine Learning (2026), Lecture 1, supervised learning and dataset construction. The Chernoff calculation also follows the setup in Problem Set 1. Course notes · Next lecture

title: Retrieval-augmented-Generation
summary: Pre-trained neural language models can learn a substantial amount of in-depth knowledge from data without any access to an external memory, as a parameterized implicit knowledge base. However, the downsides are
body: Pre-trained neural language models can learn a substantial amount of in-depth knowledge from data without any access to an external memory, as a parameterized implicit knowledge base. However, the downsides are that they cannot easily expand or revise their memory, cannot straightforwardly provide insight into their predictions and may produce hallucinations. RAG architectureEndow pretrained parametric-memory generation models with a non-parametric memory through a general-purpose fine-tuning approch: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The models leverage two components: a retriever \(p_{\eta}(z|x)\) with parameters \(\eta\) that returns (top-\(K\) truncated) distributions over text passages given a query \(x\), a generator \(p_{\theta}(y_i|x, z, y_{<i})\) parameterized by \(\theta\) that auto-regressively generates output token \(y_i\) given previous tokens, the query \(x\) and retrieved passages \(z\). RAG-Sequence Model: use the same retrieved document to generate the complete sequence. \[p_{\text{RAG-Sequence}}(y|x)\approx \sum_{z\in \text{top-K}(p(\cdot|x))}p_\eta(z|x)p_\theta(y|x,z)=\sum_{z\in \text{top-K}(p(\cdot|x))}p_\eta(z|x)\prod_{i=1}^{|y|}p_\theta(y_i|x,z,y_{<i}).\] 12345678910111213141516171819202122232425262728293031323334353637383940414243444546474849class RAGSequence(nn.Module): def __init__(self, retriever: DenseRetriever, generator: RAGGenerator, pad_id: int): super().__init__() self.retriever = retriever self.generator = generator self.pad_id = pad_id def forward( self, query_ids: torch.Tensor, query_mask: torch.Tensor, answer_ids: torch.Tensor, doc_ids: torch.Tensor, doc_mask: torch.Tensor, topk: int = 3, ) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, Dict[str, torch.Tensor]]: retrieval = self.retriever(query_ids, query_mask, doc_ids, doc_mask, topk=topk) doc_log_probs = F.log_softmax(retrieval["top_scores"], dim=-1) context_ids, context_mask = build_contexts( query_ids.detach().cpu(), query_mask.detach().cpu(), doc_ids.detach().cpu(), retrieval["top_indices"].detach().cpu(), self.pad_id, ) context_ids = context_ids.to(query_ids.device) context_mask = context_mask.to(query_ids.device) decoder_input_ids = answer_ids[:, :-1] labels = answer_ids[:, 1:] batch_size = query_ids.shape[0] repeated_decoder_input = decoder_input_ids.repeat_interleave(topk, dim=0) repeated_labels = labels.repeat_interleave(topk, dim=0) logits = self.generator(context_ids, context_mask, repeated_decoder_input) doc_sequence_log_probs = sequence_log_prob(logits, repeated_labels, self.pad_id) doc_sequence_log_probs = doc_sequence_log_probs.view(batch_size, topk) marginal_log_prob = torch.logsumexp(doc_log_probs + doc_sequence_log_probs, dim=-1) loss = -marginal_log_prob.mean() info = { **retrieval, "doc_log_probs": doc_log_probs, "doc_sequence_log_probs": doc_sequence_log_probs, "marginal_log_prob": marginal_log_prob, } return loss, info RAG-Token Model: marginalize over the retrieved documents at each generation step. \[p_{\text{RAG-Token}}(y|x)\approx \prod_{i=1}^{|y|}\sum_{z\in \text{top-K}(p(\cdot|x))}p_\eta(z|x)p_\theta(y_i|x,z,y_{<i}).\]
